' Sister Annunciata lay asleep, And all stood silent, fearing e'en to weep, Lest any shade of common, human grief ' Should cloud the tranquil spirit as it passed. But she, with long-drawn sish of sweet relief, Moved her pale lips, uncloged her eyes at last, And looked—on what 2—did crowned saint appear? Or awful vision of the Angel Seven?. The watchers lower bent their heads to hear— " Love, do I see your face again—and is this heaven?" .--TIENRIETTA CHRISTIAN WEIGHT, is Seribiter'S Magazine for June.

WATER FOR •SEREP.—Sheep requires constant supply of water. Sometimes a sheep will eat a few.mouthfuls, then go to the trough and drink perhaps a couple of swallows, then eat a little more, then drink again, and so on. It is a *stake to suppose that they do not need it. It is essentilff, too, that it should be pure and fresh. MORTALITY AMONG LAMI39.—" J. R." says e•—" I RIR losing several of my lambs, and cannot account for the cause. They are, with the ewes, eating off a piece of rape, and all very healthy; but suddenly they aretaken with a sort of giddiness, and drop down dead. The rape they are eating off was sown in September, and is now very high. Will some of your readers kindly inform me, if they can, the cause of my lambs dying ?"—Your lambs are dying from apoplexy, owing to the food being too strong for them. I should, therefore, advise you to make an alteration in the food immediately. Do you give the lambs any corn? Some bran and crushed oats would be a great help to them. Speaking in support of Lord Camperdown's Bill in favour of the provision of weighing machines for cattle at the fairs and markets throughout the country, Lord Lecenfield said that some time ago he sold a number of b.ullocks to a butcher for £l9 each, but eight others, for which he was only offered £lB 10s. per head, he retained. Ten days or a fortnight afterwards he sent those eight bullocks to the Farmers' Supply Association, through whom, curiously enough, they found their way to the same butcher. Those bullocks were sold by live weight, and he realised foss each animal £2l 19s. Bd. This repre-. sents over £27, which Lord Leconfield would have lost except for an appeal to the scales. Times are much too hard to allow us to tolerate any longer a haphazard system that leads to such injustice. NORTH LANCASHIRB NOTES.—Grass lands are decidedly behind the season, both meadows and pastures. On the latter, there is yet little to turn stock out to, seeing that they have been so closely eaten, and present prospects point to a late hay harvest, both for seeds and meadows. The continued dry weather has had the effect of making wireworm busy in the grain fields, and, there are many bare places to be seen.. An experienced friend, who has tried it, says there is no better cure for wi;eworm than a good dressing of liquid manure to the land. At the present time probably a good rolling with a heavy roller would be the best preventive, for the dry weather will have forced the pests near to the surface in search of food, and the roller would not only crush them, but give greater solidity to the roots of the grain plant. It was feared that the late frosts would have had a fatal effect upon the earlier description of fruit trees, but this has fortunately not been verified.—R. Gamma PROSPECTS IX IiP.TBI4/ AND RII3DLESDALN.— The Craven moors' embracing Skipton, Embsay, Flasby, Grassington, and Coniston, with the lesser tracts of moorland in the district, are in a condition very satisfac- tory to the sportsman. At this season of the year, when the grouse spend a great part of their time in sitting, the keepers are loth to disturb them in their occupation, and, therefore, the birds are left very much to them- selves. It has, however, been observed during the last few weeks that the birds were running about singly, which naturally led those acquainted with their habits to come to the conclusion that the mates were engaged in the congenial duty of hatching.. The old birds appear to be strong and healthy, and the prospects of good sport three months hence are highly satisfactory.—ln Upper Ribblesdale the grouse paired and nested early, and the weather, with the exception of the brief time dur- ing which there was snow on the ground, having been favourable, the incubation period has been highly satisfactory. The season is said to be fully three weeks earlier than usual, and it is predicted that when the Twelfth arrives a good many sportsmen will be astonished to find the birds so strong and bad to kill. Already some of the present season's birds have been seen about the moors, and their appearance is I highly promising. The spring has been the most satis- I factory that has been experienced for the past five or six years for all kinds of game, and not only are grouse and other kinds of winged game plentiful, but the lands swarm with hares and rabbits. Hares have put in an appearance at spots which they have never frequented before, thus providing the sportsman with an enlarged field for his exertions. An enthusiastic sportsman at Settle ventured the opinion that the coming season wll be the best for the pest ten or twelve years. This state of things applies to the great stretch of moorlands from Pen-y-Ghent and Ingleborough to Whitewell, embracing the Austwick, Lawkland, Clapham, Giggleswick, ma- ham, Kirkby, Swarth, Rathwell, and other moors. Over the greater part of this moorland, Mr. Walter Morrison, M.P., the Earl of Bective, and the Rev. M. T. Ferrer have the right of shooting, and it may confidently be predicted that they and their friends will have excellent sport.

Go and get the venison, it's 40 cents a pound, but no matter if it was 40 dollars. Let her have her way in everything till she sleeps. Then—" I ground my teeth and clenche4 my hands. "Tom, dear ! I'll rid this family of her if you will agree to what I propose." "0, Tom! I'd do most anything," said the little wife. "Then follow my instructions. I propose to move." GOOD-BYE. You are going where the sea is blue and calm, • And the soft winds only stir the lofty palm; You are going where the fire-fly darts and gleams, When the hot night comes from out the land of dreams. You are going where the white and deathly snow Never glistens, as the red sun hanyeth low; But where ripe fruit lies fainting in the heat, And the brown grass will die, withered, at your feet. Will you want to hear the wild waves dashing high? Will you want to see the White gulls screaming fly?, Will you think you hear the glad bells o'er the snow? 'Will you think of silent dead asleep below? When you stand upon the hot Pacific shore Will an echo reach you from this stormy roar? From your eyes a steady light is shining out, And it chases from my soul its last dark doubt. In that land where fireflies dance and gleam You will be mine, though 'mid the snow I dream, For love can reach beyond the ocean bar,' . 'Tis high and still, like yonder northern star. FLO. JACKSON.

div.head: THREE FIVE-POUND NOTES.
div.p: THE THREE FIVE-POUND NOTES.

Years ago there lived in Scotland a good old clergy- man who was always doing his best to help the poor as well as to advance the cause Of Christianity. At that day second-sight wail greatly. believed in. The Rev. Alexander Macklin did his best, from time td time, to 'combat the faith his congregation felt in certain seers who dwelt among them, but without much effect. ' On an occasion occurring which was a proper call upon the benevolence of the congregation, Mr. Mackin inevitably preached a charity sermon, sent round the collection boxes, or, as they were called then, the ladles, and generally offered a fine contribution to the cause. He had seldom been disappointed, and when an oc- casion of the sort one day presented itself, he entered his pulpit quite confident of the result. The sermon was a fine one, affecting some of the congregation even to tears. -The moment for the con- tribution arriving, small coin tinkled pleasantly into the ladles, and the mind of the t ood pastor was at rest, as the sum likely to be collected occurred to him. For such a cause the .three most important families in the church—the McDonalds; the McFinns, and the Calders—would certainly put five pounds each intci the ladles. In fact, he saw the members of each of these families feel in their pockets, and made no doubt of the usual contributions. - Alas! he was mistaken. When the-collection was connted over it was found to be mach less than usual. The great men of the flock had evidently not been as liberal as they were wont to be. , It was a great dis- appointment to the good clergyman, who went home with a very long face, and during the evening meal discoursed to his family about the falling off of his sup- porters. si The good wife was as sorry as he himself. The sons and daughters were indignant, and as they at about the fire in the evening, in that decorop quiet which always prevailed in the parsonage on Sibbath evening, no one was cheerful. Each, as a matter of course, held a good book in his or her hand, but I am afraid •their thoughts wandered to the delinquent Calders, Mc.Donalds, and Mc.Finns, until, as the hours for evening prayers and bedroom candles .arrived, the mother brought out the big Bible, put it on the stand near Mr. Macklin** elbow, and waited, as did the rest of the family, in solemn silence. The old servants came in and sat down near the door, and all was attention, until one after the other observed that the minister wore a very unusual appear- , ance. He was very pale, and his eyes were fixed on vacancy. He seemed to be staring with all his might at something, and to be unconscious of what was going on about him. The family were terrified, but none of them dared to speak to or arouse him; and in this state he remained for at least half an hour, when, with many heavy sighs Ind gasps, he returned to his normal condition. "I have been asleep in my chair, I believe," he said, "and nave had a very strange dream. I thought that I had gone out of doors and up the road to the kirk. The door was locked, but I did not seem to heed that,. but just passed in through the wall, and made aothing of it any more than if it was an ordinary action. I was thinking of the small contribution to-day, and wonder- ing what was the cause for it; and so I walked up the aisle and opened the vestry door, and saw the ladles all in a row on a table. 'lt's a very strange thing,' said I, that the three families should play the same trick the same day. They've had no losses, nor any offence from me, and then I saw them throw in without a blush, but just the look men have when they're doing well.' And with that I lifted the ladles as they lay 'bottom upward, and turned them the other way.and looked in. In the first nothing; in the second nothing; but in the last I saw a bit of something like paper, and, going over to where the goon shone through the window, I saw that a bit ha splintered up from the bottom of the ladle and held some bank notes pinned down, and I pave a little cry and drew , them out, and there Were three five-pound notes that had been weighed down by the pennies and halt-pence, and fastened there by the splinter." " ' Praise God!' I cried out, and awoke. It was a queer dream." "Meister !" cried Malcolm, the old gardener, coming forward, " maister, it was nae dream ye had. It was joost the second sight that fell on ye, and yell find it true, if yell gang to the kirk, for what ye saw God showed ye, and I've seen the second-sight in my ain kinsfolk often enough to ken it when it's before me. Let me gang wi' ye to the kirk, mister." "No more of such foolish words, Malcolm. But I'm not for denying that it may have been heaven-sent dream. Come away with me to the kirk, and we'll have the prayers when we come back; for my mind is not that settled that it should be to address the _Lord nst now." ' He Caught up his plaid and hat, Mal Malcolm took a lantern, and the two vventt out into the night together. The minister had. the vest.), key in his pocket, and they opened the door with this, and entered the silent room together. There on the table stood the money ladles all in a row and bottom upward, as theminister led seen them. Malcolm held the light; the master lifted the first—it Was empty. The second—that was empty too. The third—Malcolm held the lantern, closer—a it of paper eaughtthe light, and, fastened under the very splinter hr had' seen in his dream, Mr. Itracklin.fonrui three fire- pounds ntites—doubtless the gigs- of the Finns,, CaYders; and M'Donalds. fale•and trembling, he looked uovratds.Maleollo. "Phrhaps you are right and frwrong, Maltolim" he said. "Slit second sight or drearm God sent, far it was for a grind' pUrpose. Bles; His mains; we will gotome and praiie• And from that day it V ti,B said that the. Her.. Alexander-Anti/in never pre,achedlagainst the pev.ait- ing beliellivsecoad-sight. lie,! '

They are always prying into his coneerns—an offence to which I must here plead guilty; but it is no uncommon offence, and it doubtless was the innocent cause of the story—repeated, as has been remarked, without any resentment by the gentlemen at whose ex- pense it is told. A criminal was on the scaffold, about to be executed. He said good-bye to the minister and the prison governor, and shook hands with the exeeu- tioner. But to the reporters he merely nodded, saying, "I'll see you, gentlemen, later on."

div.head: MINING ROTALTIES.—No. 1.
div.p: MINING ROTALTIES.—No. 1.

BY H. WHII'HAM. A great deal of auxieti is now felt by English- men as to what the futura may have in store for them and their children, and it would seem that the most patriotic and the most practical course to pursue lies in encouraging the growing • tendency, now making itself manifest, to get at the bottom of all the incidents whch affect the land, and ren- der it difficult for England to maintain her position in the competitive struggle now being waged amongst the industrial and • producing nations of the world.' , It may be a relief to your readers to turn from, the Irish question, which, in Mr. Gladitone's words, "blocks the way,' to this other and no less import- ant question, of mining royalties,which I propose in I a series of papers to introduce to their notice. Mr. B. Pickard, M.P!, speaking at the Trades Union Congress held at Hull:- fa 1885, said "he trusted that when the delegates returned to their districts they would exert themselves to educate opinion in regardAo the evils of royalties,.so that the incubus under which they suffered might be removed." This wish received emphatic support in the loud applause accorded it by the delegates, amply justi- fying the writer in now urging upon working-men the fact that in the land question lies the great secret of all our troubles, and in also farther stating that in land-owning politicians and members of Parliament the labouring populations of our large towns have their greatest enemies. GREAT FIRES AT HAMBURG AND. PE RNAM BUCO.

HAMBURG, WEDNESDAY. 430 fire, which speedily assumed great proportions, broke ut at nine o'clock last night at the Strand and Huebener Quays. Six sheds were burned down, two English vessels—the City of Dortmund and the Gladiator—were gutted,and many others lying near lost their rigging and masts. 4-40 P st.—Another steamer, the Progress, from Goole, had. considerable damage done ts her (leek by the fires at the quays last night, but the ca,go only suffered slightly. The fire, which has now been extinguishsd, is supposed to have originated through the igniting Of Spille cotton. The &NM soon spread to five railway trucks, which were standing alongside the cotton bales, and were full of straw intended for shipment on board the Progres3. Twenty other railway trucks laden with goods which were drawn up behind the steamer were completkly destroyed. An engineer belonging to the City of Dortmund was seriously injuted. The wife and child of a bargeman wet e drowned. PERNAMBUCO, WEDNESDAY—A great Gill has occurred at Recife, the commercial quarter of this city. A number of warehouses in which 26,003 bales of cotton were st:,red were destroyed. ANOTHER LANDSLIP IN SWITZERLAND. div.head: AMERICA.
div.p: AMERICA.

Renewed eartl-quake shocks were felt at Tombstone, Arizona, on the 30t.h and 31st ult. Authentic intelligence has now been received definitely confirming the report of a volcanic eruption in the Sierra Madre durino: the earth- quake which occurred early last month in Mexico and the South-Western States. The volcano is in the State of Chih- uahua, on the elope of the Sierra Madre, near Piedras Ver- des, and continues active.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

A raid for arms has been made on Lord Ventry's pro- perty, half-way between Tralee and Dingle, seven guns being taken. The locality has hitherto been quiet, and the district is a large one, with comparatively few police stationed in it. The raid was made while the people were at mass. Lord Lansdowne, wilting from Canada in acknowledg- ment of an address from his Wiltshire tenants, says he has no reason to apprehend tlittt the attacks made upon him regarding the management of his Irish estates are likely to be sliccessful inprejudicing the public opinion of the Canadian people. -

- . The other night an attack was made on the house of some Jews in Limerick. The mob forced in the windows, and one of the occupants was assaulted. The police had to be sent for. From time to time attacks have been made on the Jews residing in the city, without any provocation. In the present instance the offenders were of the lower class.

It is stated that a Royal visit to Ireland has been decided upon in connection with the celebration of her Majesty's Jubilee. The official celebration in Dublin will be during,the last week in July, and a member of the Royal Family will attend to represent the Queen. There will be a levee and drawing room at Dublin Castle, and the occasion will be marked by conferring State honours. Dunne the past few weeks a large number of persons have emigrated from the Union of Killarney to Canada under the Government's emigration scheme. Upwards of 400 families, comprising mechanics, small farmers, and labourers, have left the distriot. This exodus has greatly relieved the local rates, which were much burdened by the support of so many unemployed persons. THE MAYORS AND THE JUBILEE CELEBRATION.—OnIy three Irish Mayors—those,of Belfast, Londonderry, and Wexford—have accepted the invitation to the Jubilee service at Westminster Abbey, but nearly all the High Sheriffs of counties are coming. Nearly 100 English Mayors have declined, on the ground that they are ex- pected to take part in local celebrations on the same day. - -

The holy well, known as the well of the Crutches, five miles from Trim, Ireland, is now being visited by a large number of people. Around the well, devotees are seen, daily 'on bended knees and barefooted, most of them havmg travelled long distances to drink the water and pray for the removal of bodily infirmities. Several 'cures," it is asserted, have been effected. In celebration of the Queen's Jubilee, Belfast will erect a School of Art, Science, and Technology, a Consumptive Hospital, an addition to the Queen's College, a Convales- cent Hospital Tor Children, and a Presbyterian Assembly Ball; while a contribution will be made, to the Jubilee Fund for the education of sons and daughters of the Irishelergy. The whole of these projects make a grand total of £lOO,OOO. Further correspondence respecting Mr. Parnell's rela. tion to his tenants appears in the Dublin Express A long letter from Mr. Kerr, Mr. ParnelPs agent, state, that Kennedy on his first farm failed to fulfil the con- tracts asto manure, and that reductions made brought down the Tent on that,farm to R4O. On the other hand, a Wicklow correspondent of the Express reiterates the -statements +which were contradicted by the Freemanss Journal.

On a panel of a window-shutter in the house of one of Or evicted tenants on the Ponsonby Estate has been found inscribed, apparently in the handwriting of the tenant's wife, these lines : I am evicted from this house, Me and my loving man, ' lam homeless now upon the world; May the d— take the plan. The panel has been cut out and sent to Cork to be framed.

Mr. James Macmanon, sub-sheriff of Clare, who was seized with an epileptic fit during the Bodyke eviction proceedings on Friday, has been removed from that office, Colonel Turner, divisional resident magistrate, having represented to the High Sheriff that in view of the repetition of these fits he would not recommend the military and police to be placed at Mr. Macmahon's dis- posal. The vacancy has been filled by the appointment of` Captain Edward Croker, brother of Mr. H. Croker, who lately went to Ennis to undertake the duties of secretary to the Clare Defence Unkin for the protection of landlords.

It is reported from Dungarvan that the Government are making elaborate arrangements to prevent any further dis- closures of official telegrams This is the outcome of an inquiry held at Cork, where it was &Loomed that a " confi- dentist" message had been diverted into the wrong channel by some person in the telegraph service. Fpecial wires are being laid direct from the Channel cable to Cork, and a cypher code la talked of.

div.head: CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.

The Liberals of Chatham have received information to the effect that it is probable that Mr. Gladstone will be induced to alter his determination expressed in a recent letter, and will take part in the laying of the foun- dation stone of the Chatham Club at an early dabe.. A Women's Liberal League was formally inaugurated at Rochdale on Saturday. Miss Cobden, the daughter of Richard Cobden, attended a meeting in the Public Hall, Baillie-street, and was presented with an address, in acknowledgement of which she made a short speech. Amongst the other speakers was Mr. R. Neville, M.P.

The foundation stone of the Glodwick Liberal Club, Oldham, was laid on Saturday by Mr. J. M. Cheetham. At a public meeting in the evening the chief speaker was Mr. Bradlaugh, M.P., who moved- a resolution condemning the Coercion Bill as tyrannical and unnecessary. He described the plan of campaign as being constitutional in its limits, free from Violence and crime, and an agita- tion creditable-to the new spirit of the Irish people. DEATH OF SIR R. HAMILTON.--Sir Robert North Collie Hamilton, Bart., 'C.C.S., died on Vonday afternoon at his seat, Avoncliffe, Stratford-on-Avon, after only one day's illness. He was born in 1802, and entered the Bengal Civil Service in 1819. In 1842 he became political agent to the Governor-General in Central India. When the Mutiny broke out he was sent with full powers to accom- pany the force under General Sir Hugh Rose. He was present at every engagement and in the field during the whole of the campaign in Central India, and for his services was created C. 8., and received the, thanks of Parliament.

Sir John Gorst, M.P., writing t a constituent, denies a statement that he was about to sever his party con- nection with Chatham, but remarks: "Many men are becoming tired of political life, so harassing, and worry- ing, and incessant are the claims which are now made upon them by the recent deadlock in Parliamentary government. Ministers who have to attend first to the duties of their office, and are then expected to be at the House from the hour of meeting till its rise—perhaps at four or five o'clock in the morning—find life hardly Worth living, and are often in the mood to retire from political life altogether."

Mr. Andrews, one of Mr. Chamberlain's constituents, writes to Mr. Gladstone urging immediate efforts to re- unite the Liberal party, and having sent the right honourable gentleman Mr. Chamberlain's answer to a communication on the mine subject, Mr. Gladstone writes—" I have seen, I think, rightly or wrongly as- cribed to Mr. Chamberlain's pr ,posal to strike out of the Irish hill the clause relating to the Irish members and to introduce into it the 'consequential amendments.' These cannot be the words intended by, Mr. W•ooding, as they might perfectly well include the virtual transformation of the measure and the destruction of its efficiency." '

a ' LABOUR REPRESENTATION IN PARLIAMENT. 1 On Monday a meeting of colliers from Wigaa, Pember- ton, and surrounding districts Was held on the shore at Southport to consider the question of labour representa- tion in the House of Commons. Mr. W. Pickard, Wigan, presided. . The CHAIRMAN, in the course of his remarks, referred to the strong necessity, from a miners point of view, for an additional number of working men in the House of ' Commons. Speaking after half a century's experience , of the mining world, and having himself been in an explosion, besides having been present at investigations into fourteen, he assured them that things would be very much altered if working-class representation were con- siderably increased in the House of Commons. (Hear, hear.) Mr. 'Pintail's's, secretary for the Organisation formed for the purpose of returning working men to the House of Commons, also addressed the meeting. He drew attention to the fact that in the Mines Regulation Bill, just introduced into the Hmise of Commons. the total number of minent was put down as 561,092, whose average wage from 1873 t 0.1883 was only about 16s. per week. These half million of miners were represented in the House of Commons by five direct members, whereas against these there were 18 colliery owners, who directlyi so to speak, represented the interest of the small and limited class of proprietors. (Slidme.) How these gentle- men acted would be seen from the recent deputa- tion sent by the colliery owners td the Home Secretary, to obtain modifications in the bill in favour, not of the working men, but of the employers. Indeed, to such length had that gone that they had used their influence to procure a clausein the bill which would practically boycott and check weigh- man who had earned the enmity of the colliers or colliery owners. (Renewed cries of "Shame.") From 1873 to 1883 one person out of every 587 in mines was killed, but in 1886 one person out of every 644 only met with a fatal , accident. That showed that the position of the miner was improved, but that was owing to the fact that in recent years the working-classes had shown an increased interest in their own welfare. (Hear, hear.) The Em- ployers' Liability Act had had something to do with thaN as well as the fact of having labour representatives in the House of Commons. Referring to the case of lawyers, he pointed out that 136 were in the House of Commons, and yet theft, were, according to the last census, under 50,000 persons engaged in- the legal profession in England and Wales. The benefits accruing from this were that the lawyers were the best protected class in the king- ,. dom. There were 800,000 agricultural labourers with- out a representative; while the whole of the landed classes had 209 members in the House of Commons, in addition to having a House of Lords. (Cries of" Shams.") The result of this was that the land was going '&4 of cultivation, and they were having to import foreign food, the consequence being that many men were out of work or were on low wages. He gave the case of the railway interest, and pointed out that 450,000 railway shareholders had 62 representatives, while 374,000 rail. way servants had not a single representative. He earneitly appealed to them to take the first step in this matter, and set an example to Lancashire.—A resolution approving of labour representatives was carried unani- mously. .

It will hardly be believed, says Society, but is no less a fact, that one of the ,few American women present at the State ball recently was seen to pocket the claw of a lobster to which the Prince of Wales had paid more than ordinary attention, The Organising Committee of the Imperial Institute have drawn up a scheme for the constitution of the governing body of the Institute consisting of 100. Ten will be nominated by the Queen, 45 represent the United Kingdom, 30 represent the Colonies, and 15 the Indian Empire, ,

UNITARTAN ASSOCIATION.—At the annual meeting of the British and Foreign Unitarian Association in London, en Wednesday, a resolution was passed heartily congratulating the Queen on her Jubilee, and expressing the hope that the future years of Her Majesty's r&gn may witness the corn- pieta triumph of the grand principles of civil and religions liberty. The words "civil and" were added to the original resolution as a protest against the Coercion Bill. ,

The representa- tives of the Press were admitted at 20 minutes to eight, and at 10 minutes to eight Mr:Wright, one of the acting Under Sheriffs, arrived at the gaol. Five minutes later Berry went to the cell of the condemned man who was in company with the chaplain, who had been present with him since six o'clock, praying and reading. The man expressed himself thoroughly penitent and hopeful. He submitted quietly to the process of pinioning, and about three minutes to 8 the procession started for the scaffold. Thechaplain walked first, solemnly repeat ingthe burial service. Following him were the condemned man, two warders, Mr. Wright, two gaol warders, and the chief warder. The condemned man walked to the scaffold with a firm step. His hands were clasped, and he fervently repeated, "Lord have mercy on me." "Christ have mercy upon me." "Oh, my God, have mercy upon me." "Lord receive my soul." In a few seconds he was upon the drop. Berry put the whitecap over his head, stepped to one side, end pulled the drop. Death was instantaneous; there was not even a quiver. An inquest was held at eleven o'clock, when the usual evidence was given.

I The annual Whitsuntide celebrations took plats at Runcorn, on Whit Monday. Fortunately although the morning opened dull and heavy, the weather bright- ened as the day progressed, and at noon, the sun. shed a bright and genial warmth. This great neces- sity of outdoor demonstrations being granted, the fee. tivities passed cif in a most agreeable manner. Al. though the inhabitenta departed •in their hundreds during the day, for Liverpool, Manchester and North Wales, there was also an iufl ix of people from the neighbouring towns, and the streets presented es scene of bustling animation whioh was made more gay by the cOnspicaous display of banner of various hues and devices in every part of the town. Owing to the feet that the Jubilee demons:ration will take place on the 21st inst., it was at one time considered doubtful whether the procession would be held on Whit Mon- day. The friendly societies With one exception deel- ded to defer their appeat mice until that interesting event, but the Sunday School authorities resolveel upon maintaining the annual custom, a resolution that gave general satisfaction. div.head: TITHE WAR••
div.p: THE TITHE WAR••

A profound sensation has been created throughout the Principality by the announcement that no further attempt will be made to effect tithe sales on any of the distraint farms without the assistance of the military, who are held in readiness. A large number of farmers and tithe-payers are under distraint in the Vale of Clwyd, Llangen, the Meifod Valley, and other places, and the farmers still express their determination to resist to the utmost unless an abatement is made on the present tithe charge. It is anticipated that before the military are sent out a compromise will be offered by the Corporation of Christ Church College, Oxford, and the Ecclesiastical Commissioners. Senoas inconvenience and delay in commercial pursuits in North Wales have been caused by the disturbances, and many curious stories of the boycotting are related. A commercial traveller representing a patent manure firm was in quest of one of the distrained farmers residing on the outskirts of Denbigh. He made inquiries for the farm, and repeatedly received careful narrations of the route, but being taken 1,, an auctioneer or appraiser he was sent a round of 15 miles. A traveller from an eminent firm of tobacconisfs was making his way into one of the dis- turbed districts and endeavoured to hire a conveyance. 'Who are you?" inquired the car proprietor. "Oh, I am chief of the bailiffs," replied the commercial gentle- man, jestingly. "Then shanks' pony is good enough ter you," was the sharp reply. "Why, can't you stand a joke ?" asked the astonished traveller. "Oh, yes," was the answer; "we are quite accustomed to jokes here, , but there's no trap for you." It was then announced over the neighbourhopd that "the man in charge of the bailiffs is here," and the unfortunate traveller was refused conveyance, food, or shelter, and was compelled to make a tour of 16 miles on "shanks' pony" carrying a heavy portmanteau. It is stated that warrants have been issued for time arrest of some of the men principally concerned in the disturbances at Llangwm Cerrigydru- dion in connection with the tithe war in Wales, and that several of the farmers and labourers in the Meifod , Valley have been summoned to appear before the justices at Llanfyllin. The Rev. E Owen has written a letter pointing out that the tithes received from Wales by Christ Church College are spent for educational purposes, and suggesting that scholarships supported from such funds should be kept for Welsh youths. An tyttempt, to sell stock which had been seized at Llangwm, Cirrigydmidion, drew together some hundreds of persons, , who showed every disposition to oppose the auctioneer and those with him. The horses attached to the carriage in which the men had come to the place took fright through the centre pole breaking, and the coach was , overturned. Then the auctioneer and solicitor, who were thrown out of the vehicle, were surrounded, and were made to sign a document to the effect that they would take part in no more distraint proceedings in that dis- trict. Bespattered with rotten eggs and with their coats turned inside out, their were escorted to a town some miles distant, whence they were despatched by train.

Two bogie engines attached to a surface-man's train, on the new line in course of construction at Stevenston, Ayrshire, came into collision on Saturday night, and 15 navvies were slightly injured, while one was so badly hurt that he was removed to the hospital.

Tbe solicitors to the Blackburn Rttepayere Aesoclation received intimation from London that a writ would be issued to restrain the Town Council from spending the borough funds in celebrating the Queen's Jubilee. The Liverpooi City council, on Wednesday, decided, by 25 votes to 18, to make a special grant of £1,500 to the Mayor for defraying expenditure in connection with the Jubilee celebrations. At its last meeting the Council re- jected a similar proposal in which the amount to be granted was £2,500.

"A.VI;;;MONDAY Ferramyi—Ricbard Hartley, aged fifty-two, overlooker in a cotton mill, and chapel-keeper of St. Ann's Roman Catholic Church, Blackburn, died on Thursday mornine from the effect, of iojuries received at Morecombe on Whit-Monday. The deceased, alonz with a party of excursionists, had ascended the cliffs at Heysham Church, Morecombe Bay, when he slipped and fell a dis- tance of thirty feet, being fatally injured internally.

I mit a robbery of the most impudent kind. Besides this form of extortion, other forms are practised. Miners are charged three- pence each for pick-sharpening, when the cost to the employer is less than one penny each ; and there are, too, deductions for school fees, arncunting to as much, in one instance cited in the Report, as 83 zd per month for the cducation of one boy. It may be asked—Why do the miners not, revolt against such tyranny ? But it is also perti- nent to ask—Why are employers permitted to do these things ? It is the duty of the law to protect the weak against the strong ; and there can be no question 'bout the duty in this instance, seeing that the evil is one which the law struck at half a century ago. There are two Bills before ParliamPnt for the amendment of the Truck Act of 1831—one brought in by Mr. BRADLAUGH, and tne other by Mr. DONALD CRAWFORD. Both Bills go to the root of the matter by prohibiting the sale of stores by employers to workmen ; by making the weekly payment of wages corn pulsory ; and by defining and limiting the deductions. Mr. BRADLAUGH'S Bill has al• ready passed the second reading; and when it reaches the Committee stage it should be possible to amend it so as to render Mr. CRAWFORD'S Bill unnecessary. It is desira• ble, therefore, that Trade Societies should make special efforts in order to bring the question at issue before members of P'arlia- ment during the recess. There will be an opportunity in many cases of obiaining, per- sonal interviews, thus ecuring, it may be, something more than the stereotyped promise to give the matter full consideration. The evil is glaring, the remedy is at hand, and there will be negligence somewhere if it is not speedily applied.

THE Liberal Unionists have been in con- ference at Birmingham, under the auspices of the National Radical Union, and the chairmanship of Mr. JOSEPH C HAMBERLAIN, but they cannot be said to have made a goodly show. There was a singular paucity of prominent politicians. Lord HARTING- TON, after his wont, sent a lett.-r ; but he does not speak of himself as a Radical Unionist, a circumstance which suggests that these fol- lowers of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN are, after all, but the section of a section, There has been a split in the Liberal party, and there is a division amongst the seceders; for it must not be lost sight of that there is an associa- tion of Liberal Unionists as well as an or- ganisation of Radical Unionists. Perhaps when they can arrree to work under some chief other than Lord SALISBURY, there may be a hope of their accomplishing something. 'At present they are powerless—except for mischief. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN talks freely enough of the support which his bantling has received ; but there is no record of the work it has done. It was perhaps judi- , cieus, under the circumstances, not to present a repot t ; not even a Radical Unionist can make something out of nothing. The member for West Birmingham still thinks pll would have gone well with the Liberal party if Mr. GLADSTONE and other leaders of the party had consented to post- pone Home Rule. A remark of this kind shows how little Mr. CHAMBERLAIN realty under- stands either the Irish question or the Eng- lish people. After a Tory Cabinet Minister, with,the consent of the Tory Prime Nlinister, had been in negotiation with Mr. PAR- NELL—an d after, too, the extension of the franchise in Ireland—there would be just as much sense in suggesting the postponement of the rising of the moon as proposing the nostponPment of the question of Home Rule. Mr. BRIGHT—and it is sad to have to write it —is uncharitable enough to speak of Mr. GLADSTONE as havintr turned his coat in de- claring in favour of Home Rule ; but all that it amounts to is that the great Liberal leader saw the signs of the times from a lofty height, and with an undimmed eye, and pre pared, like a thoughtfll and capable states- man, to accept the inevitable. When Mr. BRIGHT talks of a sudden change, and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN suggests postponement, they forget that Mr. GLADSTONE in one of his Midlothian speeches warned the na- tion that if, as a result of the exten- sion of the franchise, the people of Ire land were united ia a constitutional de- mand, it would be necessary to make such changes as would go to the very root and foundation of society. He foresaw what might happen, and what has happened, and when men litte‘Mr BRIGHr talk of a sudden change, they are simply exposing their own short-sightedness and deficient memory. It is natural for men like the once-honoured Tributte of the People to grow old and to grow conservative; but it is the crowning, glory of WILLIAM EWART GLADSTONE that as he grows older his vision clears and his mind expands ; so that while younger men "wait, debate, and hesitate,'! he is ever ready to march forward in the path of progres,,, and lead the people on from "stepping stones of their dead selves to higher things." Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, turning on Sir GEORGE TR E- VELYAN, professes himself unable to under- stand how it happens that the EX-SECRETARY for IRELAND stands aloof from his brother Unionists at such a moment: but Sir GEORGE has given good reasons for the course he has been compelled to take—reasons-which would have been equally potent with the member for West Birmingham if he had been as anxious as his late colleague to preserve the' union of the Liberal party. Mr. CHAMI3IIII- - has said of Coercion—" I hate the name; I hate the thing " ; and Sir GEORGE TREVELYAN has said as much ; but the dif- ference between the two is that Sir GEORGE gives effect to his expressed opinions by standing aloof from the Coercionists ; while Mt. CHAMBERLAIN Mocks his own words by vatting the. Coercionists on the back and vot- ing with them It is no use his pretending not to understand Sir GFoRGE TREVELYAN the country is too wide-awake' to be led astray by professions of this kind. What is unintelligible is to find JOSEPH CHAMBER- LAIN, the Radical of Radicals, the idol of the democracy, the hater of Coercion, the scorner of Toryism, the giber of " Rip Van Winkle," and the flouter of the "Skeleton of the Feast," turn tail when a constitutional de- mand is made to give the people of Ireland the right to manage their own affairs, and, belieing all hopes that were born of him, enter the ranks of the sworn foes of democ- racy, and snobbishly belaud them as " Eng- lish gentlemen " This is puzzling ; it is the riddle of riddles.

"TOUCH AND GO."
LOCAL NE WS. .
" How beautiful the rain, after the sum- mer heat"—onlv we haven't had any sum- mer heat as yet. Yesterday should have been Walking Day in Warrington. What a Walking Day it would have been !

From the way in which subscriptions for the Warrington Jubilee Fund are not coming in, it looks as if the wall in Sinkey-street will not come down, after all It would seem as if the advocates of the scheme will do anything for it but "stump up."

Brilliant weather this year has made Whit- suntide a grand holiday. Runcorn was gay on Monday with the annual Sunday School procession; St. Helens had its Band of Hope Demonstration; and Newton was alive with visitors to Newton Lake. " Laking" in con- trast to working is the right thing to do at Whitsuntide.

The fatal injury caused by a wrestling con- test in a beerhouse at St. Helens, on Satur day, was the result of an accident; but wrestling is at all times so dangerous a game that accidental injury of some kind is almost a certainty. A trial of wit is more to be pre- ferred than a trial of streng h ; but when the beer is in the wit is out.

The London and North-Western Railway Company are according their workpeople at Earlestown—some 900 in number-1 holiday for the Jubilee, and they are to have their wages as usual. Employers who can afford will please do likewise. " A fair day's pay for a full day's play" is the new rendering of an old saying, and it is as nice as it is new.

The idea of lighting beacon fires in cele bration of the Queen's Jubilee is being cor- dially taken up in the English Lake District. It is to be hoped it will be carried out suc- cessfully from one end of Great Britain to the other. As an outward and visible sign of an historic event, it is quite as much calculated to stir the imagination as many things that are proposed in the Jubilee line.

Mr. Ellis Lever, of Manchester, is deter- mined to be of service to his kind. Moved by the- recent colliery explosions, he has re- newed his offer of £soo for the production of a perfect portable electric miners' lamp within the Jubilee year. What is wanted is a lamp that shall be harmless—even when opened by a surreptitious key, or rusty nail The one bad sheep, as things go, may destroy the flock.

Speaking at a meeting of Liberal Union ists, held at Liverpool yesterday, Lord Derby said, " An Irish Parliament was im- possible, and three millions had no natural claims to override thirty-four millions." Why impossible when our colonies have Parliaments of their own, and rhen a little place like the Isle of Man can have its own house of legislature ? Three millions have certainly no right to override thirty-four millions ; but surely Lord Derby will not say that Ireland, in asking for Home Rule, wants to govern the rest of the United King- dom ?

At a recent dinner, at which a bishop was present who is known to have an aver- sion to clergymen wearing beards, some reference was made to the topic. One clergy- man with a hirsute appendage ventured to remind his lordship that Christ and His apostles were generally represented as bearded men, the only exception being—Judas Iscariot. This way of putting the case tickled the bishop's fancy; he was bowled out.

Liberals who want to keep posted up in matters political are well provided for. There are " Tne Liberal Year Book,' published at one shilling by the National Liberal Associa- tion, 83, Farringdon street, London, and "The Liberal and Radical Year Book," is- sued by Messrs. Talbot Brothers, Carter-lane, London. Both volumes contain a mass of information invaluable to politicians, but it is a matter of course to say that the shilling work is fuller than the sixpenny on.

Mr. William Crosfield has been accepted as the Liberal candidate for Lincoln. He was defeated through the abstention of the Liberal Unionists at the last election; but since then these peculiar abstainers have, by the operation of the Coercion Bill, begome small by degrees and beautifully less Mr. Crosfield is a sound and thorough-going Liberal who has made politics a study, and he will make an admirable member of Par- liament.

The people of Warrington are favoured in having so many open-air concerts, in the park, during the sumrnet months; and they are liberal in attendance if not in contribu- tion. It is rather too bad to leave it to a few to take all the trouble in the matter and provide most of the funds. If Tack when he goes with his Gill would remember the collec- tion, he would with a better grace be able to say— Here will we sit, and let the sound of music Creep in our ears.

Just when people are taking more and more to milk as an article of diet, science is mak- ing it known that it may be the means of con- veying scarlet fever and diphtheria. The cow, we are told, may have scarlet fever " mild," and the milk-drinker may" take it bad." This is not by any means encouraginz, but it is something to know that the virus is destroyed by heating milk to 185 Fahrenheit—that is by bringing it almost to the boiling point. Whisky treated in the same way does not lose its power for mischief. It will be as well, therefore, still to lay odds on milk.

THE CHESHIRE BURGLAR AND lin YA.CHT.—At Wallasey (Cheshire) Petty Sessions, on Friday morning, William Moody, the man who owns the yacht in which have been discovered proceeds of several burglaries. was brought up on remand charged with breaking into the Pioneer Stores, Sea- combe, and stealing £2B in money and other articles. He was also charged with burglary at Blackley, near Manchester,' and with another bur- glary at Knutsford. Several articles of great value were found by the police in a yacht on the Mersey belonging to the prisoner, who is only 20 years of age. Prisoner was committed to Chester Assizes for trial. Trra IMPEDING MARRIAGE OF Sin A. B. WALKER.—The marriage of Sir Andrew Barclay Welker and the Hon. Maude Okeover is to take place on the 14th inst. (says "Life"), and the vacancy which will thus be caused in the Queen's household is already being eagerly fought for. The pay of a maid of honour is not very great, only £3OO a year, and the life anything but a " bed of roses"; still the position and "the Honourable" tempt many. Sir Andrew Walker is a very rich man. The future Lady Walker will have stepsons and daugh- ters considerably older than herself, and will enjoy the novel sensation of being a stepgrandtnother at six-and-twenty. If a maid of honour marries dur- ing her term of duty the monarch gives her the handsome little present of £l,OOO. The sum, of course, will be received by the Hon„ Maude Oke- over.

GALLANT RESCUE PROM DROWNING AT WESTON PO/NT.—An act of bravery was performed at Wes- ton Point on Whit-Monday. A steamer from the Northwich district, belonging to Messrs. Verdin and Sons, had brought a human freight to Weston Point, and was returning in the evening when a little girl of three or four summers fejl overboard into the canal. In an instant, amid the confusion which ieigned on board, a. young man jumped into the water after her and succeeded in holding the little one up until a boat was lowered. The rescuer and his charge were then taken on deck, and the "Peru," for stich Was the steamer's name, proceeded on her way. Save that the clothes of both parties were soiled, no further injury resulted . from the immersion. The deliverer received hearty congra- tulations from those on board, and on the bank; of the canal, for his bravery. In the afternoon at 2-30 the teachers and scholars . rendered the sacred cantata entitled "The choicest gift," the connec- tive readings being read by Mr. R. Garnett. The singing was excellent, and the solos of Mr. Fred Dale, Mr. T. -CI uxton,. Misses- Hughes and Mainley, Misses Garnett and Plumpton. . Mr. R. E. Garnett and Mr. I. • MANPHESTER, Exnuirrrox.—Whit week lia3 seen the introduction of several novelties which have greatly added to the popular attractiveness of the exhibition. The musical programmes- have been especially. good. In addition to the exhibition band the management have secured during the week the attendance of the Blue Hungarian Band, the pipers of the Scots Guards, and the Manchester Artillery Volunteers Band. The aerial's bands with drums and fifes of the Lancashire Fusiliers, and the moun- ted band of the 13th Hussars, under the conductor- ship of Mr. Do Jong, give a grand performance of the British Army quadrilles, with the realistic re- presentation of camp and battle scenes. The Switch-back Railway is now open, and bids fair to prove one of the most popular attractions of the ex- hibition. It is situated on the western side of the park, in close proximity to the toboganning slides.. The attendance during' the week has been very large amounting on Monday to 49,873, on Tuesday to 36,355, and on Wednesday to 29,896. The provi- sions made for the amusement and refreshment of the visitors of all classes has been found to be am- ple and satisfactory: The total number of admis- sion since the opening of the exhibition on May 3rd has been 603,956. JUBILEE, CELEBRATION AT WIIITLEY.—The first Jubilee celebration that has been held in this neigh- bourhood took place at Whitley (Superior and In- ferior), near Warrington, on Whit-Monday. The idea of holding the festival on that. day originated with Mr. Fletcher, of Whitley and Warrington, who distributed free tea tickets to the Whitley Church Sunday School children and choir, to the children of the Sunday School connected with the local dissen- ting place of worship, and the choir,and to the Board School children. - The scope of the festival was sub- sequently enlarged by a committee formed of the Rev. J. J. Bryant., M.A., vicar, Mr. Moores and Mr. Mounfield, churchwardens, and Mr. Alfred Barber. These gentlemen collected donations. and by that means were enabled to give to each- of the children a Jubilee medal and a book containing an account of the life of the Queen. The children met at the Church School shortly before two o'clock in the afternoon, and here the medals and books were dis- tributed. Subsequently a short service, which was I conducted by the vicar, was held in Whitley Church. At its conclusion a procession was formed, headed by Hatton brass band, which proceeded to Spring- view, where in a field lent by Mr. Fletcher; a large marquee had been erected. There were about a thousand people on the field, a large proportion of whom had tea, which was served in the marquee. After tea the band played for dancing, and Mr. Jackson Lee, of Warrington, gave an amusing wax- work entertainment. In a second field, lent by Mr. 11. Neild, J.P., football, cricket, bowls, quoits, lawn tennis, and other games were indulged in. The wea- ther was fine, and the day was a very enjoyable one.

div.head: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.

_ On Thursday afternoon, a special meeting of this Board was held at the Board-room, Daresbury, to receive and consider the report of the committee in the matter of the claim of Mr William Leech, of Whitley Inferior. Mr Edward Greenall presided, and there ire also present Messrs Joseph Cliffe (vice-chairman), John Mclntyre, James Knowles, Tickle, Thomas Moore, John Rigby, Burgess, Aaron, Henry Cooper, P. Percival, Kenworthy, Clarke, Wil- kinson, Johnson, Beswick, Rigby, Bate, Buxton, Barber, Bradford, H. Linaker (clerk), and John Darbyshire (surveyor).—Mr. JOSEPH CLIFFE said that the committee had inquired into the circum- stances of the claim for .f.. 37 by Mr William Leech, ,for compensation for injuries received by him in consequence of heaps of soil on the highway over- turning his trap. Mr Linaker had gathered all the evidence he could, and the committee had consi- dered it well over, and taken both sides into consi- deration, and had come to the conclusion that Mr Leech should be compensated in some shape or form. Some might think £37 a large sum of money to come out of the rates. Mr Leech was as yet un- able to attend to any work, being himself attended by Dr Smith. although the accident had occurred some time ago; but, of course, it was for the Board now to decide.—Mr JOHN MclNTritz, as a member of the committee, said that he did not agree with the resolution of that commit- tee. He did • not justify the action of the IHighway Board, but denied from the evi- dence laid before them that the heaps of soil caused the accident. (Hear, hear.) There was conflicting evidence, but he was rather inclined to think Mr. Leech had gone behind the 1 soil heaps in the first instance. No one contended 1 Mr. Wright was to blame, as he was on his right I side, and gave plenty of room for Mr. Leech to pus. I —Mr. JAMES KNOWLES said they examined the road, and found there was IS feet for these gentle- men to drive in. Mr. Wright 'S conveyance took 1 seven of it, and thus left 11 feet for Mr. Leech. At the time the accident occurred they could see 40 or _ll 50 yards before them.—The CHAIRMAN said these heaps of soil had no right whatever to be on the highway, and if they left these there and the acci- dent occurred there he thought they were liable.— r. Jous. MCINTYRE : If we are transgressors all the Highway Boards are transgressors.—After some further discussion, in which several members took part, Mr. Jos. CLIFFE moved that Mr. Leech be compensated by the Board.—Mr. Bußoßss moved an amendment that no compensation be paid.—This having been seconded, was tirst put to the meeting, when 18 voted for it, only three voting for the motion.—The Clerk having been instructed to de-, fend if Mr. Leech brought an action for compensa- tion against the Board, the meeting terminated.

div.head: DEATH OF U. JOITLPEARSON.
div.p: DEATH OF U. JOITLPEARSON.

Mr. John Pearson, chairman of the Lancashire / and Yorkshire Railway, died on Thursday night, at his residence, Golborne Park, Newton-le-Willows. The late Mr. Pearson was a justice of the peace for the city of Liverpool, had been Mayor of the borough, and High Sheriff of Lancashire. He began life as a working engineer in Liverpool, and was well known as an exceedingly skilful mechanic in connection with steam engines. He became asso- ciated with Mr. Knowles, who used to be an under- viewer in *collieries. At this time a number of Liverpool people, including Mr. Grant Morris and others, invested their money in the then very little unworked Wigan coalfield. Mr. Pearson's mechani- cal knowledge then became of excellent use, and the firm of Pearson and Knowles, so well known in Warrington and Wigan, be- came one of the most prominent in reference to the supply of, coal in Lancashire. They under- took successfully contracts for the supply of coal and cannel to the Government of the day, their means developed, and at the time when coal rose to an extravagant price they succeeded in having al- most a monopoly of the supply to the different rail- way companies and the large consumers of Lanca- shire. The result was that the firm amassed a large sum of money. Other companies, however, de- veloped so much that the firm was a few years ago made into a limited company—the rCarBoll and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, Limited. Mr. Pearson was in politics a Conservative, and in that interest was returned to the Liverpool Town Council, eventually becom- ing an alderman and Mayor of the borough. From 1875 to 1876 Mr. Pearson was High Sheriff of Lancashire, and during his tenure Of office his hos- pitality to the judges and the Bar was a matter of congratulation with all concerned. Mr. Pearson became chairman of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company only recently. Before Mr. Pear- son's accession to power the Lancashire and York- shire Company, although they had been the great cotton-carrying passenger medium in Lancashire, had become somewhat indifferent to the large carrying ,power which 44y before them. During Mr. Pearson's chairmanship, however, the traffic was developed, and new lines were organised. In private life Mr. Pearson was the most hospitable of men, and his hospitality took a wide range. Al- though he never took an active part in politics, he had been solicited to become a candidate, along with

I Colonel Blackburne, fcr.:lie representation ofe.outh.. West Lancashire. This, however, he declined, as he did also in reference to very strong invitation to become a candidata for Liverpool. at the last general election.

Mr. Brooka seconded, and Mr.. Maltby and others.supported the proposi. tion, which was carried unanimously.

div.head: WARIIDIGTON DEPUTATION.
div.p: A WARIIDIGTON DEPUTATION.

Yesterday, a deputation consisting of Messrs R. A. Naylor, Claud J. Morris, John Pierpoint, J.P.. and J. C. Hutchings, proceeded from Warrington to Manchester, to lay before the direotors of the Man- chester Ship Canal a proposal to increase the pro. cted dock accommodation at Warrington. The deputation was appointed by the General Committee which has been appointed to promote the interests of the Canal in Warrington at a meeting of which we gave a full report in our last week's issue. On the arrjval of the deputation at the Ship Canal offices in Manchester, it wits found that, owing to some misunderstanding, there were only two directors present, namely, Mr, W. J. Crossley and Mr. J. IC Bythell, together with the secretary, Mr. Whitworth, some of the prinoipal directors and the chief engineer, Mr. Leader Williams, being in London. No definite decision, therefore, could be come to with regard to the proposals of the deputation. The two direc- tors present, however, received the suggestions of the deputation with some favour, and expressed a, desire to meet the wishes of the Warrington people to the fullest extent, provided that they would not be under the necessity of going to Parliament for further powers, or involved in too great an expendi- ture. They agreed to lay the proposals before the full board of directors, after which a decision would be come to.

GRAPPENHALL BAND OF HOPES ANNUAL FESTIVAL. Thu Grappenhall Baud of Hope is an organisation which, in an unobtrusive way, has done a great amount of good in the neighbourhood of Grappen- - hall and Thelwall. The annual festival in connee. tion with the organisation took place on Thursday in beautiful weather, and, it being the twenty-fifth one that has been held, special interest attached to it. Early in the afternoon a procession consisting of .about 300 persons was formed, and, accompanied by the Lymm Church of 'England Temperance So. ciety's band and the Grappenhall drum and fife band, it marched through the villages of Thelwall and Grappenhall. Some beautiful flags and ban- Inerettes, with suitable mottoes, were carried, and amongst them was the old flag of the society,which headed the first procession twenty-five years ago. The children of the Band of Hope were provided with a tea by Miss Naylor, on the lawn at Cuerden Hall, and afterwards games of various kinds were indulged in on a field lent by Mr. Erlam. Several of the banners carried in the procession were opt. cially worked by Miss Jefferson, of Thelwall, and they were greatly admired. After the children had been regaled there was a well attended public tea in the Thelwall Temperance Hall, at which the fdVA lowing ladies assisted at the tables :—Miss Martin (Altrincham), Miss Moyle, Mrs Rover (London), Mrs R. Garnett, Mrs Carter, Miss McLean, Mrs Harrison, Miss Naylor, Mrs John Naylor, Miss Jefferson, Miss Okell, Miss Thorne (Peterborongh), Mrs Shakeshaft, Mrs Miller, Mrs Kinsey, Miss Hough, Miss Brown, Miss Gleave, and Miss Hall. In the evening a meeting was held in toe Temperance Hall, at Thelwall. It was td a very attractive character, a varied programme of considerable interest having been ar- ranged, and the Hall, a commodious one, was crowded.—At the commencement of the meeting Mr. R. A. NAYLOR an- nounced that the chair would be taken by their esteemed .friend, Mr. W. J. Martin, of Altrincham, nod the proceed- ings you'd be opened by the singing of "We come to-night a little band of temperance girls and hue." That having been done, the Rev. J. B. Richardson, of St. John's Church, watedoo, offered up prayer.—The choir then sang a glee, after which the Camameer, who was received with en- planes, addressed the meeting. He acid it was about twenty years since he first came to Thelwall, at the request of the late Mr. and Mrs. Naylor, and he believed that a great amount of good had been the result of the principles which since then had been so ably advocated in that village by Mies and Mr. Naylor. (Cheers.) He believed he was right in saying the present Was the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Grapcenball Band at Hope (cheers) and it was a very good opportunity for those Who signed the pledge at that time and no doubt there were some such present —to celebrate that evening their silver wedding. He felt a debt of grati- tude to the Church of England Temperance organisation for the place it WAS now taking in promoting the work el tem- perance. At one time that organisation looked somewhat coldly on that qneation, but now it WAS doing as good a work in this direction as any other society that could be found. (Cheers.) It must be remembered that during the last twenty-five years they had received much good advice. Might that advice be acted upon, and might they all press forwaralrin the good werk of temperance. (Cheers.)—" The Warrior Bold" WAS then sung by Mr G Boner, and Master Price recited'Victoria's Jubilee." Mr. Ihin (Warrington) sang "The maid of the mill" in an excellent manner, and a short address was then given by the Rev. J. B. Richard- son, who remarked that the afternoon bad been a very pleassnt one. That night they celebrated their twenty-fifth anniversary as a Band of Hope Temperance Society, and this yen was also the twenty-fifth anuivereary of the Church of England Temperance Society ; that was a very pieta tat coincidence. They were met that night for a great purpose, and he trueted that each one would try and stem the tide of intemperance. He earnestly asked these who, although not addicted to taking intoxi- cents, were not pledged teetotallers, to become each for the Bike of example. He did not think any man was doing his full duty in the world unless he took some interest in the 'great temperance crusade that they were carrying on. (Cheere.)—Mr. G. Shakeehatt having given two violin solos, end Mr. Baxter having sung "The old brigade," Mr. R. A. NAYLOR gave the results a a competition in connec- tion with the society for prizes for the best cottage gardens. The first prize of £1 was divided between John Edwards wad Joseph Lord, and the others were awarded as follows: —2nd prize, 78 61, Charles Harding; 3rd, ss, Mrs War. butte. ; 4th, 3s 6d, L. Foote ; sth, 2s ad, Thomas Parr. There were nine competitor,. Mr. Nayler remarked that the cottlgers deserved great credit for the way in which they managed their gardens. He thought that it was far tetten that they should spend a few shillings in flowers, and a little spare time in their gardens on an evening, than that they should spend their time and money at a peblic- house. He expressed himself as being highly gratified at the suecees that had attended that twenty-fifth anniversary, aed hoped that some of these present would join in the Jebilee celebration of the society twenty-five yens hence. —Mr. Ikin then gave "Goodbye, sweetheart, goodbye," and the usual votee of thanks b:ought the meeting to a conclusion.

For more than a month I coeld not sit down nor get up without the most intense agony, and,l was suffering all the while A friend of mine, who is a doctor on one ef the Transttlantic linertedvised me to go oat of the regular channels and try a remedy that was becoming quite famous Inv the remark- able cures ir was effecting; but my prejudice was alto- gether too strong for that. However, I did quietly begin trying the remedy, but I promise you I said nothing to my brother pies sicians or even to my family about it. Yet, sir, it Was a revelation to me, lor in all me, medical experience I never saw anything operate so rapidly or so effectually as that did. I owe my health to-day, fir all I know my life Mee, to the remedy known as Warner's Safe Cure. That was tbe starting point for m and nay prejudices faded very rapidly after that. lem assure you I went to reading extensively, and is &mils .ing mire exteneively, and I sup- pose lan elysed all the toiling proprietary medicines that are made. Many ei he in I found perfectly useless, being compeuneeei simply of oa.er with a little flavouring to taste, the majority of them I found, however, mach up of pre- scriptions ueed by physicians in their every-day practice. ' After discovering this. I said to myself, 'Why should the medical fraternity be prejudiced against these prescriptions, whirl, they are writing every day, simply because they are put up wholesale and sold with a Government stamp on the wrapper.' I saw its manifest absurdity, and ; resolved that I would be bound by it no longer. Since that time I have prescribed proprietary remedies nearly , every day in my practice, and I have no reason to regret , having done so, Why, only a few days ago I advised a lady, I who wee suffering from serious female difficulty, to use this same Warner's Site Cure which cured me. I saw her this morning, wed eke is quite well. We have no right in the medical fraternity to sit back and declare there is no such thing as improvement or advancement, er that we have a monopoly of the remedies which nature has given to man- kind. There are great changes going on in every depart- ment of life, and there are great developments in medicine as well. Thoneende of people die every year from sup- posed typhoid fever, rheumatism, or other complaints, when the fact is they are simply the symptoms of disease. It is a well-known tact that the vast majority of diseases arise from , imperfect kidneys or liver. The liver becomes clo tg,td and its work is thrown upon the kidneys, they become over- worked and break down, and so the poison gets into the blood instead of being thrown from the system. No one with perfect kidneys or liver is ever troubled with rheuma- tism or gout, and it is the poisonous particles which these diseased organs allow to get into the blood that clog the capillaries of the lungs and cause tubercles and consump- tion. Thousands of children die every year from dropsy as the equal of actrlatina, when in reality it is dese teed kid- neys!, which have becomed weakened by the fever they have just passed through. Here is another strange thing. Not one in ten people who have diseased kidneys notice any pain in the vicinity of the kidney', for these organs hive very few nerves of sensetion, and lose what little they have when they have become diseased; and the symptoms are shown in hundreds of other ways." .6 Well, doctor, you have got some new truths here, cer- tainly, but they seem very reasonable to me." 6. It was officially announced on Thursday that Prince Albert Victor will visit Dublin as the representative of the Queen at the Jubilee celebration on the 27th inst., when a military review and banquet will be held. Trim MANCHESTER UNITY A M.C.—The business of the Annual Movable Committee of the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows was commenced on Monday at Dover. In his opening address the Grand Mister (Mr. J. J. Stocktll) con- gretulated the members upon the continued increase of the Unity, which now numbered 655 000 members, including 38,063 juveniles, and had a capital of £6,3oooOo—The committee resumed its sittings at Dover on Tuesday morn- ing, when the reports of the committees which considered the directors' report presented on Monday were received. Among the recommendations of the committees was one to the effect that there should be much stricter superintendence for the Unity. The proposition of a delegate to have the rules printed in Welsh was not agreed to.

NOTES BY THE WAY.

The report and statement of accounts of the War- rington Football Club, which have just been issued by the hon. see., Mr. J. E. Warren, and the hon. trea- surer, Mr. T. Pemberton, are documents of interest to the innumerable supporters of football in Warring- ton. Mr. Warren's report is well arranged, succinct, and full of matter; and Mr. Pemberton has so manipulated his voluminous accounts—which must have involved no end of trouble in the keening of them—that one can not only see at a glance the present financial position of the club, but also its present position as compared with former years. During the last four or five years the club has, financially as well as in other respects, made very rapid strides forward. In the season 1882-3 the receipts were £34 3s 1041 ; 1883-4, £45 4s 21; 1884-5, £l9O lOs 74 ; 1883.8 £Be9 es 71; and in the last season no less than £1,234 2s 44.

Ttie secretary reports having arranged firat team matches for next season with Aspull, Barrow, Free Wanderers, Moss- ley, Broughton, Manchester Rangers, Broughton Rangers, Rochdale Hornets, Wigan, Kendal Hornets, Kendal, Dews- bury, Oldham Wakefield Trinity, Rugby, Halifax, Moseley (Birmingham), and deckmor.dvike. With regard to the scoring by members of the first team Barnes stands a long way ahead of any other player, having dropped eight goals and secured twelve tries. The next on the list is Massey, with one dropped goal and four tries. Speaking of Barnes's remarkable record, Mr. Warren says that he cannot find that it has been beaten by any player in England during last season.

Rain spoiled the match at Oxford between the Univet- eity men and the Lancashire c ieketers, which ended on Saturday i4n a draw—greatly in favour of the latter. The Ltncashire innings, in which 132 runs had been scored overnight for the loss of three wickets, finished off just after luncheon for 247, giving the county team a lead of 103 runs. A single inn;bigs defeat was averted by some capital batting, and when the match was abandoned as a draw the score stood :—University, 144 and 105 for four wickets; Lanca- shire, 247.

The mach between Yorkshire and Warwickshire at Huddersfield on Saturday also ended in a draw, and when stumps were drawn Warwickshire hid only three wickets to fall, and had 36 runs to obtain, to save a single innings defeat. Another fifteen minutes' play would probably have given Yorkshire a most decisive victory. Score :—Warwickshire, 95, and 35 for seven wickets; Yorkshire, 168. Middlesex has received a crushing defeat at the hands of the Surrey eleven, the game brought to a conclusion on Saturday a( Lord's ending in a victory for Surrey by an innings and 70 runs. Score—Middlesex, 81 and 134; Surrey, 291. The contest between Kent and Gloucester- shire on the same day resulted in a draw, the score being:— Gloucestershire, 181; Kent, 202, and 155 for six wickets. Elevens representing North and South met at Lord's on Monday to play a game for the beet& of Walter Price, of the Marylebone ground staff. In their first innings the South totalled 61, and in the second they fared little better, being out for 82. Ties North made 99 ha their first innings, and won the match by six wickets. The Lancashite County team on Tuesday beat a team of Eighteen Colts, at Manchester by an innings and 11 runs. The colts exhibited poor form. On the same day York- I shire were victorious over Kent, at Sheffield, by four wickets.
