div.head: MINE
div.p: MINE
THE EX
SAITTRI),AT, JUNE 4, 1887.
TIIE );ItYN COLLIERY EXPLOSION.

THE INQT4ST. An explosion of fire damp, wbrloh, had it happened during the ordinary hours of work, would probably have cost mazy lives, occurred.ahout eight o'clock on Thursday night week at Messrs. Richard Evans and Ocr's Bryn Colliery, Ashton-in-Makeafield. Those who survive were Ant made aware of what had happened by •learing a rug:lin:r noise, and then feeling a strong -current of air which carried them-it considerable dis- tance, and in the words of one of the men, "knocked as about a deal as long as we had our senses." At the time of the explosion eight men were in the pit— "lamely, George Prescott, John Harrison, John Lowe, Joseph Lowe Peter Clare, John Ryan, and .John Laughent, all furnacernen, and Joseph Houlton, a firmest, Ryari sustained a severe scalp wound and many braises. John Lowe, a Middle•aged man, of Edge Green. Was killed, cad Peter Clare, of a)lborne, and John Harrison, of A.shton.in-Makerfield, suc- cumbed from the effects of the explosion and after damp, Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy county coroner, opened an inquiry at the Bryon Hall Hotel, Brynn, on Mon- day, on the bodies of the three deceased men. Mr. J. 0. Swift, St. Helens, solicitor to the firm, watched the ease on behalf of Messrs. Evans.—Rachel Holmes, a married wozan, of Edge-green,idestified the body of John Lowe, her father, who lived at 6, Edge-green, Golborne. He was fifty years of age last birthday. He was a collier employed at Bryn Colliery, and went to work 23 usual on the 20th inst. as a shot-ligliter.— By a Juryman: She never heard her father say there was any gas in the place. He always felt satisfied as far as she knew.—Eliza Harrison said she was the wife of John Harrison' and lived at Ashton-in-Makerfield. She had identified his body now lying at the colliery. He was a shot lighter, and thirty years of age. He went to work about four o'clock on Thursday after- noon. When she next saw him on the following day he was lying dead. Witness, asked whether her has. band ever complained about gas in the pit or the boles not being properly drilled, answered in the negative. —Esther Glare, wife of Peter Glare, of Cfolborne, having identified the body of her husband, said he had been engaged at Bryn Colliery as head shot-lighter. He was forty•five yearn of age. Dmeased went to work at a quarter t..) four o'clock on Thursday after- noon, and she had not seen him until that day (Mon- day), when he was lying at the colliery.—By a Juror: Her husband rammed the shots and another person lighted them. He had been employed at the colliery about seven years, but had not been brought up as a collier.—A Juryman (to witness) : Did your husband ever complain about his place not being safe P—Wit- nes.] : He never said anything about his work to me. —Did he ever say the holes were not properly drilled? No, not t 9 me.—At this point the Coroner said be was obliged by law to adjourn the inquiry, in order that Mr. Hall, her Majesty's inspector, could be present: Mr. Hall WriS down in the pit, and had hem there several hours, making a minute examination of the workings. By mutual agreement the inquiry was ad- journed for a week. The bodies were at once removed from the colliery to their respective homes, and the funeral of Harrison took place on Tuesday evening at Aehton-in•Makerfield. Crowds of persons visited the colliery on Sunday, and much sympathy is manifested/towards the sorrowing relative'.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON. MIN:YESDAY.

There is just now a cloud hanging over Mir. Glad- stone of the existence of which very few peoole are aware, It is well known that, greatly to the de- light of his hoe, of admirers, he has declined a peer- age. But there is one honour looming over him with respect to which he has no option of refusal. Any day he may become a baronet, and the w„lendid simplicity of "Mr. Gladstone" will be alt: to"Bir William,' and he will take rank with the Lard Mayor and some of the Queen's favourite family doctors. His brother, Sir Thomas Gladstone, second baronet, has a son a captain in the Coklstreant Guards, who seemed to stand between Mr. Glad- stone and the devolution of the title. But Captain Gladstone recently broke a blood vessel. and the state of his health is such as to cause much anxiety to his friends. He is not married, and in the event of his death following upon that of the old baronet nothing could save Mr. Gladstone from the inflic- tion of the title. Sir Thomas Gladstone is now in his eighty-third year, and in the ordinary course ,of things cannot expect to outlive his younger , brother.

The Gladstones have always been a long-lived ,race, and, bar accidents, there is every prospect that Mr. Gladstone will reach the age at which his elder 'brother now stands. If this expectation be realised be will certainly accomplish Ins heart's desire and will see Ireland free, prosperous, and happy. Whether Mr. Gladstone lives or dies, Ireland will get Home Rule. He has set the ball rolling and no power on earth can stop it from reaching . its ulti- mate.goal. But Mr. Gladstone hopes not only to be privileged to lead tbe Liberal army to the verge of the promised land, but to enter it with them, and personally participate in the triumph. Those most intimate with him do not doubt that his hope will be accomplished. He has a pathetic habit of allud- ing to his advanced years, hinting that the close of his labour is now at hand. This has induced in the public rand a certain feeling that he is breaking down. But, neither physically nor mentally, is there any indication. of such catastmphe. With the exception of a weakness of the voice, he is still in the very prime of his powers as an orator. His bodily strength is something remarkable. Herbert Gladstone is well known as an athlete. He care- fully keeps himself in training, and can do almost i anything n the gymnasium. The other day, when some remark was made as to his prowess, Mr. Glad- stone gravely announced that with a little train- ing he would baek himself against Herbert for a wrestling match, or a walking match, and there were some present who would noi have given odds on the youth. Herbert Gladstone's prowess, more particularly on the cricket field, has often been pub- licly manifested. It is well known that his elder brother is one of the best football players in Eng- land, though nobody would think it to look at him as_he lounges through life.

Mr. Brig& has more than once announced his re- tirement from public life, and has yielded to pres- sure put upon him to reconsider his determination. He has once more made it known to those imme- diately concerned that he will not again contest Birmingham, and this time, I fancy, his resolution will be found irrevocable. It is easy to understand that he is sick of public life. It is a melancholy end to a great career, and though Mr. Bright is, as usual, convinced that he is right, and that every- body who differs from him is criminally wrong, he cannot be insensible td the peculialety of his political posilion, or to the severance of personal friendships. He never was very polished in his observations with respect to persons from whom he differed. Through a long lifetime his present - friends and allies, the Conservatives, were the butt of his conversational vituperation and the object of his public attacks. Now, it is his old friends in the Liberal party and his old colleagues on the Front Bench against whom the slings and arrows of his vitriolic condemnation are directed. It is amazing to hear the savage way in which in pretty mixed com- pany, and in rather public places (such as the smoking room of the Reform Club for exam- ple), he discusses the action of Mr. Gladstone and those who stand by him. Mr. Bright, as his conversation makes clear,has not forgotten and can- not forgive the Irish members for their personal attacks upon him in times past. What has been said of him has been nothing compared with the buckets of foul abuse poured over Mr. Gladstone by some of the very, men who now exalt his name. Mr. Gladstone, however, is big enough to sink a perso- nal feeling in the sense of public duty. Mr. Bright unfortunately is not. In connection with the recent proceedings in the Courts of Law, and the unexpected turning up of a youthful heir reported to be dead, there has arisen the inquiry what has become of de Tourville? About ten years ago a jury sitting at Bodsent in the Tyrol, found de Tourville guilty of murdenng his wife, and was condemned to be hung. Subsequently the sentence was commuted to one of penal servi- tude for life. It is said that de Tourville was either released or escaped from prison, and has been seen in London. Colonel Ouvry, C. 8., who takes a special-interest in the case, has sant me a narrative printed for private circulation, which tells more about de Tourville than is generally known. In 1867, when this man first appeared on the scene in London, he went under the name of Perreau. He had made the acquaintance of a young lady named Brigham, who had a considerable fortune, and only , erre encumbrance—to wit, her mother. Perreau married her, and a year later Mrs. Brigham was shot dead with a pistol, which her son-in-law ad- mitted he had handed to her, but said it went off accidentally. An inquest was held, and tLe jury not being satisfied that there was evi- dencq against Perreau, returned a verdict of accidental death.'-Perreau thus became master of his wife's fortune. In 1871 she, too, died "of ph th isis pulmonia," as Perreau reported, By this time Perreau had changed his name to de Tourville. He had a son born in 1869, whom, according to the pro- secuting counsel in the murder trial at Bodsen, he attempted to get rid_of by setting fire to the room in which the child was sleeping. It is this boy, re- ported to have been drowned at Naples, whose un- expected turning up in the flesh varied the course of the action heard the other day for the disposition of the de Tourville fortune.

What brought de Tourville into a position of European celebrity was the tragic end of his second wife. In 1875 he met in the Tyrol a lady named Miller • the daughter of an English captain. Miss Miller was forty-seven years of age, but by way of com- pensation, she had a fortune of £70,000. Be Tour- ville proposed marriage and was accepted. A few months after he took his wife for a holifay tour in the Tyrol. Leaving. his hotel for a walk, he presently returned with the pews that his wife had fallen down a precipice—accidentally, as he averred; murderously pushed over, as everybody on the spot believed. It was for this crime that de Tourville was tried and found guilty. Meanwhile, in his compulsory confinement, and in the absence of the heir, the fortune left by his first wife has been accumulatin2, and efforts made to • appropriate it were foiled by the reappearance of the heir. But where is de Tourvills ?. This is a question which this remarkable domestic tragedy, as far as it has gone, leaves unanswered., Ni Just before the hitsun holidays interposed, we were in the high season of another kind of myste- rious disappearances, which will doubtless manifest itself again next we i week when the season enters upon its last course. This s the disappearance of hand- some opera cloaks, new bats, and anything special in wraps, which may be worn at great receptions. Scarcely a day passes but the London papers have advertisements addressed to the lady who "took by mistake" the fur-lined cloak, or the silk shawl, and who is asked to return it to a given address. These little incidents may, of course, be the results of mistakes. But the mistakes are very frequent, and, oddly enough, it is invariably a partieu-

div.head: WARRINGTON ASSESSMENT _ COMMITTEE.
div.p: WARRINGTON ASSESSMENT _ COMMITTEE.

A monthly meeting of this body was held at the Board-room, at the Workhouse, yesterday morning. Mr. J. Rylands presided, and there were also present the Rev. G. P. Roberts, and Messrs. Pennington. Blackhurst, W. Houghton, J. Bough- ton, J. Swinton, W. Owen ,(valuer), and J. C. Sutton (clerk). TIN VALUER'S REPORT.—The VALUER (Mr. Owen) re- ported that since the last meeting he had made the follow- ing valuations as instructe2 :—(1) Messrs. P. and W. Skel- ton, new shop premises, llorsemarket-street, Warrington •, grass £lB6, rateable £l5B. This did not include the old buildings behind, which were useless. (2) Messrs Itylands Brothers. Limited, iron building, Church-street, Warring- ton. This assessment of gross £9B and rateable £BO, had been appealed against. After going into the matter be was of opinion that the value now should be gross £55, ratea- ble £44. The stable assessment, which was Row at gross £l7 103, rateable £l5, should be raised to gross £25, and rateable £2l. (3) Messrs. Galway, Bainbridge. and Co., engineering works, Lythgoes-lane, Warrington. This was an appeal at the last meeting. The valuer said there was now no beneficial occupation of the premises, with the exception of the offices,which were detached from the foundry and fitting shops, and he suggested that an assessment for the office of gross £lO, rateable £B, would meet the case. (4) Township of flaydoek. In this township he found the assessments, with few exceptions, correct; further information would be Obtained with respect to. the exceptions. (5) Messrs. Richard Evans and Company. According to instructions, the valuer had looked into the assessments of the collieries in the townships of Bavdock, Newton, and Burtonwood. All information was vouchsafed him' and he was permitted to examine the certified accounts of Royalties paid on the coal raised fur the veer ending the 4th April last. The understanding arrived at with the c mpany some years ago was that the Royalty should be taken as their assessment, and that in addition to this there should be an amount put upon the works and tire railways. The assessment on the works and railways at Haydock was £1,090, which he saw no reason to alter; the assessment on the coal he found should be £6,697 13s 83, instead of £5,956 19s Bd, which ap- peared in the list signed at the last meeting. It. the township of Newton the railway lines were ascessed in three different items, amounting alto- gether to gross £440, rateable £4OO, which there was DO reason to alter. Tne assessment on the coal would have to be materially increased. It was at present £l5O, and the amount of coal- got in the township of Newton, after deduct- ing for wayleave to the township of Haydock, should be £1,203 19s Bd. Under the township of Burtonwsod no coal had be,en got for the last twelve months, and the: e would, consequently, be nc assessment. Ins VALUE OF PUBLIC-HOUSE PROPERTY. Mr. JEN- KINS, solicitor, made an application on behalf of Mrs Bal- -1 straw, landlady of the White Ball Inn, Horsemarket-street, for a !Auction of the assessment on that building. 'the gross rateable now was £BO, and the nett £72, which repre- sented the rest. The rent had been reduced. Acting on his advice the tenant pointed out to the Brewery Company that she was unable to carry on business successfully under the conditions on which the tenancy was held, and the Brewery Company thereupon reduced the rent to £7O. Mr. Jenkins contend,d that Mrs Balshaw was unable to succes:- fully carry on business on the present assessment, and that on that account she stiou:d have consideration. It was notorious that the vtlue of licensed houses had much de- creased during the last few years.—After some discussion the matter was referred to the valuer to report upon
WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of this body was held at the Board-room at the Workhouse yesterday morn- ing. The chair was taken by the Rev. G. F. Roberts, and there were also present Messrs. Z. Armitage, T. Jolley, W. Houghton, G. Grange. H. Owen, J. Houghton, R. Kilshall, J. Swinton, W. Owen (Sur- veyor), F. Kerfoot (inspector of nuisances), S. Sutton (clerk), and Dr. Sephton (medical officer of health). SURVEYOR'S REPORT.—Tbe SURVEYOR, in his monthly re. port, wated that during the month inspections had been made of the following buildings :—Dr, Gornall's house, Grappsnhall ; Mr. J. Tildesley's houses, Wellfield-street ; Messrs. Taylor and Craik's houses, Manchester-road; Mr. Millingtoo's houses, Penketh ; Mr. Bratinhall's houses, Litch(ord ; Mr. Mounfield's houses, Manchester•road. The following plans for new buildings had been submitted, and might be appioved :—The Hon. Leopold W. H. Powys, Paddy Horse, Hoed-lane, Great Sankey; the execators of the late Mr. Peter Rylands, Shippon for 10 cows at Massey Hall, Thelwal I ; Messrs. Lever Bros, extension of shed at Bank Quay. VVarringron.—Adopted. MICJICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—The repett of the medical officer (Dr. Sephton) stated that the returns for the month ending May 31 were : births, males 21, females 11; deaths, males 11, femtles 7. The death rate from all causes was equal to 18 1 per 1,000 against 72 the corresponding month of last year. The deaths under the zvmotic class were due, one to measles, at Grappenhall, and one at Burtonwood to dipthoria. In the latter case he (Dr. Sephton) had suspected that the water Was the factor, for, upon eau:lining the pre- mises he found the well which supplied that and five other houses with water situated at the edge of the brook, and the wat-r from the bed of the brook ran into the well. The drainage from several houses was emptied into that brook about twenty yarde higher up than the well. Consequently the sewage must find its way into the well. He suggested that a specimen of the water be submitted for analysis. A case of diptheria had been reported from Orford. He would recommend in this case that notice be served on the onner to removr; the closets and build proper cesspools; or adopt the pail closets; also disconnect the elopstone pipe from the drain, and put down trapped gullies to the Nerd drains.— The report was approved. THE SEWAGE OF PENICETTL—The CLERK read a nom. municition from the Local Government Board asking Whether the Authority were now in a position to submit plans and sections for the proposed alternative scheme for the disposal of sewage at Penketh. He (the clerk) had written to Mr. Rontledge, whose reply to the effect that the plans would be ready shortly, lead been forwarded to the Local Government Board.

Rs APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFrcsit. On the mo- tion ,7f Mr. JOLLEY, seconded by Mr. Anstimos, it was resolved that Dr. Sephton be re-appointed Medical Officer of Health for the ensuing year, at a salary of £BO per annum.

Twit PAIL SYSTEM. The CLERIC read the report of a committee appobited to meet the Sanitary Committee of the Corporation on the subject of the removal and cleansing ef nails, Sm. At a preliminary meeting, held on the 20th ult., a report was read giving the number of pails, privies and ashpits, and the c^st of keeping them in order. Within the extra municinal portion of Warrington there wee 130 pail closets and 420 privies and ashpits, or 550 in all ; the present cost to the ratepayers was £54. or rather lees than 2s per annum in respect of each. At a subs quent meeting the deputation were introduead to the Stni,ary Committee, and Alderman Burgess, chairman of the committee, stated that he had caused ingairies to be made, and found that in all there were 142 pails within the district Their sub-committee had come to the conclusMn that it wr uld take £l5 to put tbe _pails in reasonable repair. This amount would be required in the first instance, and they calculated that the work of removal, cleansing, and replacement, and keeping the pails in proper condition, would cost 12s per annum in respect of each. Mr. Owen pointed out that the present coat averaged 2s per annum in respect of each pail or privy, but Alderman Burgess was of opinion that the committee could not charge a less sum than 12a without doing an injustice to the borough rate- payers.—A diacusaion followed the reading of the rep.art.— Mr. lILLEY slid that he should not like the Author4y to agree to the terms mentioned. He thought that they might give instructions for the tubs to be put in proper repair, and for the cleansing to be properly carried out.—Mr. R. OWEN and other members also expressed themselves averse to agreeing to the terms suagested, and it was finally agreed that the committee should confer with the contractor on the matter. This was the principal business.

Goon TEMPLARY.—The weekly sessbn of the members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars wan held on Monday evening, when there was a good attendance. Brother T. Martindale, W.C.T., presided. A number of visitors from the A.nhton Excelsior Lodge were in attend- ance. After several items of lodge business had been tran- sacted, the evt fling's programme "Entertainment," was pro- ceeded with. Brother Barnard gave a reading entitled "It won't hurt ;" Brother John Taylor sang "The old teeto- taller ;" Brother MA,tioddle real " Our children ;" Bro. Uren sang 9'fha rose ;" Brother Newman gave a reading; Sister Minty song " Lillie Dale ;" Sister M. E. Clarke s ng one thing thou lackest ;" Brother James Blinston sang " Tna warri.)r's boy.;" and Sister Jane Clarke sang " 11%r away." The selections were all well rendered, and the evening wan pleasantly spent.

Smith is in mourning, for her hus- band, and now,. when she plays the piano, she strikes only the black keys. The man who is in the wrong uses hard words and soft arguments„ while the man who is in the right uses soft words and hard arguments. "Bridget, did you get the flowers that 'lam to wear, to-night in my hair "Yes, mum; but----" "But what ?" "I've mislaid the hair, mum!" A MEAN RETORT.—Jenks—" Ha, ha,, ha! That's, a, pretty good story, isn't it,. Binks ?" Binks—"-Very good." Jenks—" I told it well, too; didn't I?" Binks • —" Well, I think my nurse used to tell it better." Total abstinence. from food is said to be a sure cure for rheumatism. It is. not stated how long a sufferer must abstain, but we shouldthink an abstinence of six, months would cure the most obstinate case known to medical science. Maud, if you sheuld• make as good a "catch" as lam said.to be ?—Maud Throw it back again, Charley. "Why, Mrs. S., is this ,you.—and in mourning? at hadn't heard that—that—' "Yes. Mr. S. was laid l at rest two weeks ago." "I am so shocked. Was his. death a sudden one?" "Very; without warning. He died of a cold contracted only the day before., Acen't the shops lovely ?" " I wonder why wringing the hands is always such am expression of sorrow!' exclaimed a young lady to her bashful beau. "It isn't tit isn't !" he cried, as he slipped. an engagement ring upon her finger; and. added: "The ' ringing ' of a hand is often the prelude to the ringing of bells—wedding bells." She gazed upon the "solitaire" and smilingly said: "Let 'em ring." UNKIND co THE AmATEUß.—Amateur Actor (after the play): "I am surprised to see you here to-night,. Miss. Smith. I understood that you always gave up amuse- ments during the Lenten season." Miss Smith: "Oh,. I do. I wouldn't think of attending an amusement of any. sort until after Easter." 'A FISHY EXPLANATION..—When Lord Erskine was admitted a member of the Fishmongers' Company he made an after-dinner speech on the occasion. On coming home he said to a friend, "I spoke ill td-day, and stammered and hesitated in the opening.' "You certainly floundered," was the reply; "but I thought you did so in eompliment to the fishmongers." OPTIMISM.—" Reuben," said Mrs. Ttubbs, laying down the evening paper, "what is meant by optimism " Optimism? ' " Yes ; the paper says that optimism is not a characteristic of the modern age?' "Optimism, Hannah, is a disease of the eye, and you'll git it the lust thing you know, if you keep on a-reading that fine print." MASHING A MASHER:—A. young masher walking up and down the platform of a railway station in Scotland with a companion who had come to see him off observed two handsome girls enter a first-class carriage. "Look here," he said to his companion, who did not 'pay much attention to his dress—" I'll get into that same compart- ment, and I'll tell you what I want you to do. When the train is about to start, you come up and touch your hat, and say to me, 'Mr lord, the guns and dogs are in the van.'" His companion smiled assent, but said he doubted if he could do it with the proper air of a noble- man's servant. The masher took his seat with a lordly air in the same carriage with thissoung ladies whose interest he wished to excite. The moment arrived and the train began to move, when his companion came up to the carriage window. "Hey, Jock," he shouted, "tell your moister to be sure to send thae breeks o' mine by Saturday !"—the young masher having to reconcile him- self as best he could to being regarded as a tailor's aP- prentice. One of 'the most amusing papers in the April maga- zines is contributed to the Century by Mark Twain, who, ' under the head of "English As She Is Taught," presents a marvellous array of answers alleged to have been made by pupils in American "public schools" to their teachers. A future citizen of the United States defined a Republican as "a sinner mentioned in the Bible." Of the mathematical samples we prefer the ingenious defi- nition of a circle ,as "a round straight line with a hole in the middle;" of the geographical, the assertions that "Russia is very cold and tyrannical," and that "Ireland is called the Emigrant Isle because it is so beautiful and green." The pearls of history are numerous and precious—e.g., 'by the Salic law no woman or descendant of a woman could occupy the throne." and "the Middle Ages come in between antiquity and pos- terity." As a specimen of literary history, take the statement that "George Elliot left a wife and children who mourned greatly for his genius." The science of " physillogigy is to study about your bones, stummick, and vertebry." It teaches, for instance, that the "gas- tric juice keeps the bones from creaking." A member of the tight-booted fraternity was out, relates a writer in the Sporting and Dravtatic News, one terribly cold day in December, and had done nothing but ride about in the rain and hail. Finding his legs turned to ice so far as his booth reached, and the points of his knees sodden with cold and semi-frozen rain which chilled him to the bone, he pointed for hdroe. Arriving at a public-house on the way, he took a glass of raw spirits to instil a little heat into his frame, but he was disfladed from repeating the dose by an old gentleman in boots which covered two pairs of woollen stockings —wet enough, but warm. He pointed out that to supply the upper storeys with heat and to leave the lower de- partments in cold was to drive the blood to the head, &c. If you must have whisky," said he, " buy a bottle and get, it outside of you. Pour it into your wet boots, which I see are fearfully tight and causing you great suffering." And he did. lie purchased a bottle of the dew of Ben Nevis, and he poured half the contents into each boot, which had the effect of re-creating a warmth in his lower extremities. But this salutary proceeding excited the wrath of some labourers, one of whom re- marked," It's time we had a halteration Look at that bloated haristocrat hactually a-pouring Heaven's blessed licker into his boots, while we poor beggars can't get a sup! It's enough to make a cove turn revolutioner !" His LITTLE JoKE.—Mrs. Sardonicus—"l see here in the paper that the Irish children have to go barefooted in the winter. I think that's dreadful, don't you?" Sar- donicus—" Why, not very. Igo barefooted at least a ' third of the time myself." Mrs. Sardonicus—" I just wish you'd tell me when you ever went barefooted in the wintertime?" Sardonicus—"Why, Igo barefooted o' nights." ON THE DELAWARE.—Passtnger—" The Vanderbilt yacht was launched near here was she not?" Deck- hand—" Yes, ma'am, jest below here, to Willington." Passenger—" Let me see, what is her name?" Deck- hand— Alphy,' ona'am. It's one o' them heathen words, an' is took from Alphy an' O'nigger; meanin' fust come fust served." •Nor SHE!—The papers have" given accounts of an aged cook who has just succeeded to an income of some- where about thirty thousand pounds a year. Of course she has been interviewed. The reporter was rather as- tonished, when, in reply to his remark, " Ah, you will be able to keep a cook yourself now!" she answered ironically, "Not if I know it." That cook knows some- thing. A PRACTICAL DEFINITION.—" What does' transparent' mean?" asked a Scotch Board-school teacher lately of his class in the third standard. After a long pause, he almost despaired of getting an answer, when suddenly an urchin with a rough head and dirty face cracked his fingers excitedly. "Well," said theteacher encouragingly. "My inither, sir." "Your mother! Dear me, how so?" "Because," explained the neglected boy, "when my father cam' home the ither nicht, he said to my mither, Ha, my leddy, I see through ye noo ! ' " As; AGED COUPLE.—A lady who has taken a cottage in an out-of-the-way place called at a small farmhouse the other day, and asked the farmer's wife if she could ret her have a fowl. " Yeou ken have a pair, mem," was the reply. "But I only require one," remarked the lady. "Sorry, mom," said the farmer's wife, "but this there pair as yeou see a-roomin' about is the on'y fowls we hey -left. They hey lived together since they were chickings, some 18 year ago, and I arn't a goin' to part 'em fur yeou nor nobody, thpugh times is hard." THE PRINCESSES AND TiR COTTAGER.—A good many years ego, when Queen Victoria was spending a short time in the neighbourhood of the Trossachs, the Princesses Louise and Beatrice paid an unexpected visit to an old female cottager on the slopes of Glenfinlas, who knowing that they had some connection with the royal household, bluntly ejaculated, "You'll be the Queen's servants, I'm thinkin' ?" "No," they quietly replied, "we are the Queen's daughters." "Ye dinna look like it," was the immediate reply of the unusually outspoken Celt, "as ye hae neither a ring on your fingers nor a bit gowd i your lugs." Sir,—lf "X" is eary anxious to hasten on the time to prepare the fatted calf, to celebrate once more the return of a solid united party, I will advise him to give his aid and ability in educating the Gladstonian section of the party—io restoring back the old principles which the Liberal party , has always boasted-6.7, viz.:—To ensure the safety ire the weak against the s rang; to give freedom to business peo- ple to trade with all who desire to buy, and to rive freedom to all who wish to buy at any shop where they desire, with- out let or hindrance. As a Liberal, I have always regarded this to be the only plan whereby we can be prosperous. No , prosperity can exist-es long as things ge on as at preernt in Ireland, let the laws-be ever so good. If there are grievance@ there is nothing to stand so the way of redress kylegitinaate agitation, without tryisrg to I force them down the threats of the people by intiaridat!ou, and winkisg and rejoicing at murders, and driving the people to desperation to sueb an extent that people whoare outraged are compelled to submit to it owing to their being afraid to give evidence-agaicst those who have cruelly outraged them, and brought them to ruin. Then, again, I woota like to ask X" bow bwcould rejoice by partaking of the-fatted calf, if the good andatrue-hearted Litrirals of Ireland were absent,struggling against an Executive Government set over them against their will? "X" might be able to rejirice over the fatted calf underthese conditions, but I cannot believe that a single Lib,ra? Unionist could rejoice under suer con-, ditions, no matter what temptations may be placed inltheir way. know there are cany business men and property ewners in Warrington who are supporting Mr. Gladstone in 'the present crisis, who -would pull a long face if they were driven into the position in which many are placed:in Irolco.d, for it is well known that hundreds of shopkeepers in Ireton:l, who are compelled to-show their sympathy for the Nakona: League,,and subscribe to its funds, are looking forward wit:. impatience for their promised freedom.—Yours, &c.,

•LYMM 'LOCAL BOARD.

A monthly meeting of tia Board wie held at the Offices at tymm on Thursday evening. Mr. H. Cameron presided, and there were also present Messrs Thomason, Forster, ißreziindale, Dutton, and T. J. Ridgway (clerk). MISCRLLAIIIZOTI6.—The Board heard and decided upon eeveral appeals made by residents against their rating.— The usual monthly reports of the surveyor were read and coulirmed.—The Clerk read a letter from the county ear- ‘veyor asking if the Board intended to renew their contract fru-the repair of county bridges, which would expire on the 110th of August, for a further period of seven years. The Clerk explained that-the,letter had reference to the bridge at the top of the Dam and the oontract was to. pay Ns gsyear. It wee decided to renew the contract. .

ILY3III AND Tag Sum 'CANAL SCRIM —The Clerk -stated that a requisition had been signed by a number of the ratepayers of Lyman, addressed to the chairman of the 'Board, asking him to call a meeting of the inhabitants with a view of assisting the directors of the proposed blanches- ter Bblp Canal to raise the required capital. Be (the clerk) did not know that it was really necessary to bring the matter befo-e the Breed, but,as it was addriesed to the.chair- man, it was only right that the Board should know shoat it. He had written to the directors with reference to the ex- po3ses )1 holding a meeting, and had intimated that he did not see how the Board .I:amid pay the expenses out of the rates. A reply had, however, been received to the effect that they would pay expenses He bad also written asking what night would be best salted for the holding of the meet- ing, and the reply had been received that Wednesday night would be the beat, and that a depu,ation would attend. This was the principal Wiliness.
WARRINGTON WOREENG-MEN'S BUILDING SOCIETY.

!La.st evening the annual meeting of the members 'of .the Warrington , Permanent Benefit Building Society was held in the Golborne-street School- room. There was,a_ good attendance, amongst these- present being Alderman Harrison and Mr. John Halton (trustees) ; Messrs. James Harding, E. Wal- lington,,E. Fenton, R. Isherwood, J. W. Bouchier, J. Bsxter, J. Bradshaw, and W. Bodle, junr. (managers); Mr. Peter Dalton (secretary), Alder- man .11,arrison was elected to preside.

:THE CEAITEHA.N'S REMARKS. In alew opening reanarks, Alderman HAnnisox. said it seemed almost incredible that seventeen years had passed since the first meeting of that society, but it was something to say that it had maintained its position ever since that, time. It had had difficulties to contend with it had had enemies, :in a sense, to contend with—adverse reports ;had been spreadiabroad, but notwithstand- ing all :that had been .sad that club maintained its position, and he thought the report that would be read to-them that night would give an encourag- ing account of the progress the society had made. Althovgli they had lately- been living in depressed times that society held its awn, and he was sure it possessed .a .reputation that was unassailable. He believed that its funds and everything in connec- tion with its management would bear comparison with the best managed institution in the town. (Hear, bean) He believed that whatever money had been advanced by the soeiety had been ad- vanced with the prudence and cautiousness neces- sary to produce a good investment and to secure for the shareholders the advantages that they had. a right to expect from good management. (Hear, hear.)

" Oun MUTUAL Farzien."—This is the title of a little monthly magazine, the first number of which 'has just been issued under the auspices of the War- rington Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Society. According to the editorial preface the object aimed at is to place in the hands of subscribers a payer which will be interesting, instructive, entertaining, and edifying, and in the first number this object is fairly attained. The contents are• varied, among other items being a story entitled "A terrible ex- perience," a brief article on Socrates. under the heading of "Men of fame," and a dialogue on the Divine existence. There are also scientific notes, a poetry column, a aerial story, and a number of local notes or paragraphs. An article by the Rev. J. Howell Jones, on "University correspondence classes" Will be read with interest. Altogether this little magazine is a very creditable amateur produe-, tion, and is likely to make an opening for succeed- ing numbers. BURGLARY IN SANKEY,STREET.—At the Borough Court, on Monday, a tailor named James Ashby, last from Chester, was'remanded for a week on a charge of having, between the night of the 26th and the morning of the 27th of last month, burglariously entered the dwelling-house and premises of Messrs. Jesper and Co., tailors, Smiley-street, and stolen from the workshop a brown coat two black worsted morning coats, and six pairs of tailors' scissors, Value .£7 105 in aIL He was also charged with hay- ing entered the workshop of Jame&Critchley, tailor, Irlam-street, and stolen two pairs of scissors, of the value of 4s. Prisoner, who had recently been work- ing at Messrs. Jespees, is alleged to have entered tha premises with duplicate key. He was appre- hended at bole, near Chester, by Detective Inspec- tor Brittan, of the Cheshire County Constabulary, and then had in his possession property that has been identified as having been stolen. YESTERDAY'S POLICE BUSINESS.—The business at the Borough Court was unusually light yesterday morning. There was only one prisoner, a man named Charles Russell, who was remanded as a deserter from the 3rd Hussars (E. Troop), stationed at Manchester. A woman named Mary Hill sum- moned Mary Cogan. a neighbour, for using threaten- ing language towards her, and the defendant was ordered to pay the costs of the summons. On the prosecution of Mr. Garnett, school attendance officer, George Travis was fined 58, in respect to two children, and Richard Hodgson lOs in'respect to two children, for not sending them regularly to school. At the Occasional Court, yesterday morning, a young woman named Mary Goulden, of Penketh, was brought before Mr. Tinsley on a charge of sleeping in a stackyard at Orford, and of doing damage to a quantity of straw. She was sent to prison for three weeks—seven days for vagrancy,. and fourteen days for committing the damage. Mtrew rig THE PARK.—On Whit-Monday evening the band stand at the Park was occupied by the St. Paul's Sunday School .Band, which, under The leadership of gr. Robert Smith, played a varied selection of dace music. There was a large num- ber of people present, many of whom indulged in dancing, and the music was listened to with evi- dent pleasire. On Wednesday evening a selection of music was played by Fletcher's Band, and there was again a large attendance of the public. It is stated that it is intended during the season to asphalt the space immediately round the band stand, as well as the walks leading to it; and that, as many complaints' have been made of the unsuitable provision for the players, a new stand will be erected during the next three or four weeks. Next Monda37 evening the St. Paul's Sunday Schools band will Play a selection of dance music in the park, commencing at 7-15. THE TREAT TO SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHERS. The treat which Mr. John Crosfleld intends to give the Sunday school teachers of Warrington and their friends, in connection with the Queen's Jubilee, is likely to assume much larger dimensions than was at first anticipated. Aire fdy over thirteen hundred tickets have been issued by Mr. George Riley, and it is expected that still more will be applied for. Given fine weather, the gathering at Walton Lea is likely to be a most enjoyable one. • Every prepara- tion is being made by Mr. Crosfield to provide for the convenience and entertainment of his guests. It is intended to erect a marquee in the grounds, in which about five hundred persons can be seated at one time, and provision will be made for dancing, lawn tennis, and other gamm and amusements. The gardens and conservatories will be thrown open and, as they are exceedingly well stocked and finely kept, will no doubt be a source of much pleasure to the visitors. "HARVEST" AT THE PUBLIC HALL.—Some high- class acting has been witnessed during the present week at the Public Hall, the performers being Miss Birch's London Company, and the play Mr. H. Hamilton's "Harvest. It is admitted by those who have had the pleasure of witnessing a performance of this piece that the high praise which was be- stowed upon it when on the London stage is not exaggerated. In tone it is pure and elevating, in quality original and thoughtful, and, in develop- ment before an audience it is fascinating and soul- stirring. On each evening the audience was warmly appreciative, and the efforts of the actors were frequently rewarded with hearty applause. The caste includes the following ladies and gentle- men, viz. :—Miss Gladys Ffolliott, Miss Venme Ben- nett, Miss Lilian Ellis, Miss L. Arson, and Miss Clara Birch; Mr. C. K2Cooper, Mr. 0. Stuart, Mr. Boling- broke, Mr. F. Hawley, Mr. W. Lowe, and Master C. Falcon. Last evening the performance was in befits- fit of Miss Birch, and was under the patronage of Col. Thackwell. There was a good attendance, in- eluding a considerable number of the military from Orford Barracks. The condluding performance will be given to-night (Saturday.) WHIT-SUNDAY AT ST. MARY'S CATHOLIC CHURCH, BUTTERMAIIKET-STREET. The different services held at this church on Sunday were well attended. The solemn mass at eleven o'clock in the morning was celebrated by Father Corlett in the presence of a large congregation, the sermon being preached by Father Carew. In the evening at kialf-past six the Rosary was recited and different English hymns sung, after which a sermon was preached by the Superior of St. Muy's, Father Sumner, upon the portion of the Cree "I believe in the Holy Ghost, the Holy Catholic Church," which was listened to with great attention by an audience which filled the large church, many having to stand throughout the service, The annual May procession round the church took place, headed by cross bearer and acolytes, followed by the different guilds' connected with the church. Some very beautiful *banners arrived last week, which have been' purchased for the procession on Jubilee day, and were carried by young ladies, the designs of the banners causing much admiration. Other improvements have lately taken place in St. Mary's Church by placing the gates to the entrance of the chancel adjoining the marble rails. The gates are a splendid specimen of the metal-worker's skill, and are another step to- wards the completion of this fine "church. The grand organ is now being made by the celebrated organ builder, Mr. Edward Franklin Lloyd, of Liver- pool, and is to cost £l,OOO. div.p: TELE 41TATEXENT OF ACCOUNTS.

The SECRETARY fead the following statement of accounts, viz. :—The managers have pleasure in lay- ing the seventeenth annual statement.of accounts before the shareholders, as shown in the annexed statement. The sum of £1,475 is 8d has been re- ceived as subscriptions during the year, and £1,439 I7s Id for repayments, making the total receipts £2,914 18s 9d. The withdrawals during the year amount to £1,405 Is 2d. The sum of £1,325 has been sold to members during the year. There are 187 subscribers holding 269 i shares, and 3it bor- rowers holding 130 i shares, making a total of 221 members holding 399 i shares. The profits for'the year, after deducting working expenses, amount to £3OO 13s Bd, out of which the manage:s recommend a dividend of 4 per cent., which will take £270 Its 9d, leaving a balance of £29 18s lid to be carried forward to next year's &counts: The reserve fund amounts to £350, and the contingent fnnd to £5O. The whole of the managers retire. Messrs. Hard- ing, Wallington, Fenton, Isherwood, and Bendier are eligible, and offer themselves for re-election. Six additional managers will be taken from the register in rotation.—On the motion of Mr. F. JOLLEY, seconded by Mr. T. HALL, the statement of accounts and balance sheet were adopted.—The recommendation of the managers that a dividend of 4 per cent, be pail was agreed to on the motion of Mr. FENTON, seconded by 'Mr. NrAir.

ELECTION OF MANAGERS, &C. Messrs Harding, Wallington, Fenton, Isherwood, and Bouchier were re-elected managers on the pro- posal of Mr. HALL, seconded by Mr. EDWARDSON ; and in place of Mr. A. Rathbone, who had expressed a desire to retire, Mr. J. Baxter was appointed.—On the motion of Mr. ISHERWOOD, seconded by Mr. Warrntrount, Mr. J. E. Wright and Mr. Thomas Domville were re-elected surveyors of the society. --Mr. W. Ford and Mr. I Leeson were also re-elec- ted auditors on the motion of Mr. POTTER, seconded by Mr. MIL.—On the motion of Mr. HALL, secon- ded by Mr. COOLEY, the managers were allowed 6d per head for their attendance at each'meeting dur- ing the past year.

div.p: LIVERPOOL EXHIBITION.—The promoters of this exhibition advertise special attractions. Accom- modation is provided for 300,000 persons, promenade concerts are held daily, and the grounds are bril- liantly illuminated, Among othei attractions are old Lancashire houses, an electric fountain, the " Eddystone Lighthouse," three hundred feet above the level of the sea, and trophies of war, and mementoes of famous explorations. Combination tickets, which include admission to the exhibition, tramway fare, and a trip on the Mersey, are now being istued at one shilling each. div.p: WARRINGTON.

WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.—A. sitting of this Court was held on 'Thursday, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes. The cause list comprised seven adjourned plaints, 805 original plaints, and 47 judgment summonses. The only case of interest is reported in another column. Tat VoLowrEm3.B.—On Saturday the Warrington volunteers, to the number of about 350, assembled in full dress at the head-quarters, and later on at Arpley Meadows, a flu .de joie was fired in honour of the anniversary of Her Majesty's birthday. The officers present were Colonel Greenall, illajorO'Leary (Adjutant), and Captains Thompson, Ridgway., Buckton, Baynes, and Widdows.; and Quartermaster Hutchinson.

ENTERTAINMENT.—On Tuesday evening a very successful entertainment was held in connection with the Brick-street Independent Methodist Chapel. There was a good attendance. The object of the gathering was to raise funds for the purchase of crockery, tables, and other requisites for the hold- ing of public tea meetings and other social festivi- -ties and the arrangements for the meeting were made by ladies, who collected subscriptions, pre- pared a tea, and carried out an excellent diusical programme at the entertainment, which took place ,after the tea meeting. ISCHOOL EXTENSION IN SILVER-STREET. Much needed additions to the accommodation of the Wes- leyan Schools in Silver-street have recently been completed. They consist of a new classroom and the extension of two old classrooms, in accordance with the requirements of the Edueetion Depart- ment; the new classroom has been opened into the old one, and the two together form a very good room for meetings; when the folding shu.,i;er division is fixed the rooms will afford good accom- modation for Sunday school purposes. The heating of the schools 'la about to have attention, and will be remodelled on the newest prineiple. The work has been in the hands of Messrs. Collin and on, from designs by Mr. William Owen, Cairo- street.

--"iHE--- Jumrutz Ft:rm.—At a meeting of the aubi- lee Executive Committee, held under the presidency of Mr. T. Monks, on Tuesday -evening, it WAS re- ported that the number of Sunday school children who'woifid take part in the procession would pro- bably exceed 13,000. Under these circumstances, the Committee agreed that, as the funds at present stood, they would be unable to carry out the entire programme, if sixpence per head were to be allowed to each of the children. • It was therefore resolved to recommend the General Committee either to re- duce the sum per head or to make an allowance for a certain number of children. It was also decided that the medals shall be distributed to the children on the day of the procession, when they assemble at the Town Hail. An advertisement in another column names the Sunday schools to which it is at present intended to give Jubilee medals. Superin- tendents of the schools, who have not already done so, are asked to send a return of the number of scholars, boys and girls, who attended on the last Sunday in .April, to the mayoress, Cedar Lawn, Latchford. It is also stated that medals will be given to the Sunday school children only, and that teachers will not be included. DEATH OF A LICENSED VICTIJALLER.—Mr., John Bickerstaff, landlord of the Golden Grove Inn, Lyme-street, died on Saturday morning_ after a long and painful illness, which he bore with much resignation. The deceased gentleman, who was 71 years of age, had been attended by Sir William Roberts, of Manchester, Mr. Bickersteth, of Liverpool, and Dr. Fox, of Warrington. The late Mr. Bicker- staff came to Warrington about 40 years ago, and succeeded is uncle at the Golden Grove. He was much respected for his integrity of character; and his quiet and retiring disposition endeared him to many. His private charities were extensive, many in pecuniary difficulties having been by him gene- rously assisted. In politics he was a Conservative and he was a member of the Church of England. The funeral took place at the cemetery on Wednes- day, when the body was followed to the grave by many relatives and, friends, including several mem- bers of the Licensed Victuallers' Association. The coffin was supplied by Messrs. S. E. and R. Johnson, of Bridge-street and Rylands-street. It was cov- ered with wreaths &Imposed of choice white flowers. he funeral arrangements were under the care of Messrs. J. and W. Dutton, drapers, of Sankey- street: A large number of persons witnessed the funeral procession to the cemetery. FOREIGN COMPETITION. At All Saints' Mis- sion, on Sunday, the prizes, consisting of books, to the Sunday school scholars, were distributed by Mr. and Mrs. T. Morris. In addressing the children and their parents and friends, after the distribution, Mr. Morris remarked that it was a pleasing duty to him to give books away, especially to youths who had just left the day schools, and had commenced to earn their living by becoming the workers in the various workshops and manufacturing industries. , He all to the People's Palace the Queen had just opened in the east end ef Loadon,comprising as it did all sorts of material for the education and amuse- ment of the people. If it lay in his power, and he had the means, he would have a library and a tech- nical school in every district where the population was large enough to admit of them being made use- ful. The Americans and the Germans never tired of pushing such institutions upon the notice of their: I people, who took advantage of them very much to their profit, and to this country's loss. Whilst we were saying "'e will try and do this or that," the people named did it, and so walked over us. He contended that unless our youths had the oppor- tunity to learn how to saw a piece of wood, or weld a piece of iron, as the youths of other nations had, there was nothing for it but for us to be be- hind in the world's race.

Idarly . handsome ,and -valuable piece of appa- rel that disappears. The facilities for such enterprises are wide ,enough. At some of the big houses, whose doors are periodically opened in .the season, from a thousand to fifteen hundred people flock. There aze servants in the hall who take wraps, for which a ticket is given corresponding with another of the same number which is pinned to the property. It would seem that only to the bearer of the voucher would the wraps be given up, and such is the intention of the plan. But when towards midnight the crowd flock down the staircase and take possession of the cloak- room chaos setsin, and the alertand practised thief. who seems to make a good living in his line of busi- ness, can take anything she pleases without fear of detection. The police are on the alert, but, from the very naturo of the cirwnstances, the case is sur- rounded with difficultieT, and which up the present time have baffled Scotland-yard.
